In the case of biology related projects, students have three choices: a research project (worth 30 credits), which can encompass laboratory based experimental investigations, field studies, field experiments and so on; an investigative project (worth 15 credits), which can include analysis of previously acquired epidemiological data, nutritional surveys and analysis, mathematical modelling of biological processes and so on; as an alternative, students can take the Project skills in the life sciences module (worth 30 credits).

This module focuses on response of the nervous system to injury focusing on the peripheral nervous system and spinal cord. Detailed organisation of the peripheral nervous system, spinal cord including pathways and relevant higher brain structures will be covered. Pathological mechanisms and plasticity of the system will be examined. Topics will be covered in the context of experimental studies to develop understanding of current research strategies in the laboratory and clinic aiming to lessen effects of such injuries and facilitate neural regeneration and functional recovery.

This module will focus on developing understanding and critical thinking in the area of cognitive and clinical neuroscience. Teaching will include disorders of perception, attention, memory and basal ganglia disorders (Parkinson’s disease). As well as discussing cognitive abilities like attention and emotion, while covering technical methods like EEG and brain imaging (fMRI). The lectures will cover the theoretical basis of each method and its application to clinical research.

How can we convey the importance of science and research to people who haven't studied scientific subjects? Why is it vital to do so? What is the difference between communicating science and involving the public in science?
In this module you will explore different approaches to engaging the public in science, with an emphasis on biological and medical sciences. You will look in detail at a range of examples of public engagement such as museums, broadcasts, social media and schemes that involve patient groups in medical research. You will critically assess who they are designed for and how well they work for different audiences. Examples will include some of the unique public engagement activities offered by QMUL. Based on what you have learned you will then develop and undertake a public engagement object/activity yourself. Teaching for the module will include face-to-face sessions, online resources and site visits. Assessment will be through coursework.

The aim of this module is to provide students with the opportunity to conduct an original research project in the field of neuroscience. This is a practical-based module wherein students conduct original research supervised by an academic member of staff through the academic year. Students are required to explore the background of the research and its rationale, construct hypotheses to be tested, learn necessary skills with which to conduct the work, compile results and analyse them. They will write a dissertation including critical analysis of literature, reporting of experimental design and results as well as their evaluation.

An experimental investigation involving laboratory work, normally resulting in a piece of original research in the area of pharmacology and therapeutics. The work also involves critical evaluation of previously published results. A dissertation is prepared describing the research work undertaken, and placing it in the context of other research in the field. The student also gives a short oral presentation on their work. This is a compulsory module of 30 credits and will be presented as a report not exceeding 6000 words.

This module explores human hereditary disease in terms of genetics, pathogenesis, clinical features and clinical management. We will look at key examples of chromosomal abnormalities (i.e. Trisomy 21), monogenic disease (e.g. cystic fibrosis, Huntington's disease and Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy) and common disease (e.g. coronary artery disease). Students will be introduced to methods and techniques for identifying genetic loci associated with disease (e.g. homozygosity mapping, genome-wide association studies, DNA sequencing). Finally, we will discuss issues around genetic screening, testing and counselling.

This module is designed to equip students with the essential academic skills to successfully complete their degree, identify strengths and weaknesses so as to identify how best to flourish in Higher Education. The module focuses on scientific writing, study skills, critical thinking, and English proficiency, all together supporting the development of effective learning strategies throughout their academic journey in the Nanchang JEI. Students will learn to access and evaluate scientific information and understand lecture structures and develop personal authoritative writing. Being well integrated with other technical modules, it ensures students gain foundational competencies for academic and professional development. Delivered across two semesters, it includes Academic Skills lectures, workshops, and English Support Tutorials.

The concept of the cell progresses to an introduction to theoretical aspects contemporary microscopy. The basic organization of eukaryotic cells is introduced including structure and function of membranes and the nature and function of the different organelles. The cytoskeleton is introduced together with how it allows for cell movement and contraction in specialized cells, and how cells communicate. The diversity of cell junctions and the organisation of cells into tissues is presented ending with an introduction to stem cells. Specialisation of different cells, in particular those sampled for testing, will be emphasised.

This module aims to provide students with a broad understanding of the cellular and molecular basis of hereditary and non-hereditary human diseases caused by genetic lesions. Students will learn the interaction of genes and environment in causing diseases and will get an understanding of how laboratory techniques can be applied for diagnosis of diseases caused by genetic abnormalities, ranging from Mendelian diseases to cancer. Students will then appreciate how the identification of specific genetic lesions is important for diagnostic, therapeutic and prognostic purposes.

All cellular properties, activities, inheritance, metabolism, structures and behaviours rely on biochemicals. Thus an understanding of the fundamentals of organic chemistry, the chemistry of carbon, is required to understand cellular life. In this module we will cover the fundamentals of chemistry from atoms and bonds through to the structure of macromolecules. To understand genetics and the central dogma, the chemistry of DNA, RNA and proteins will be introduced. The basics of molecular interactions will also be raised to understand how molecules lead to cellular events and changes, and taken together, this comprehensive introduction will prepare the student for learning the specialist Genetics, Cell biology and Biochemistry and other molecular and cellular modules.

Medical ethics underpins clinical decisions but a fundamental knowledge of the ethical considerations coming into play is essential to underpin the entire healthcare and diagnostic backdrop leading to these decisions. This module will introduce the student to the four pillars of medical ethics in healthcare provision. An understanding of how medical ethics influences decision making in aspects of medical research, clinical laboratory science, data science as well as professional behaviours in the workplace is discussed in an interactive manner.

This module aims to provide students with a broad understanding of the human cell and cellular and molecular basis of hereditary and non-hereditary human diseases caused by genetic lesions. Students will learn the interaction of genes and environment in causing diseases and will get an understanding of how laboratory techniques can be applied for diagnosis of diseases caused by genetic abnormalities, ranging from Mendelian diseases to cancer. Students will then appreciate how the identification of specific genetic lesions is important for diagnostic, therapeutic and prognostic purposes.

The module introduces python programming language and its use in data science. This module introduces the student to Python coding and the Jupyter Notebook and data version control. In addition a fundamental understanding of a range of data structures and flow control features, modules, classes, data visualisation, input/output, and simple data analysis libraries are covered during the module. These may also be applicable to other programming languages that the student will encounter.

This module builds on the skills introduced in year 1 and focuses on developing scientific writing, critical thinking skills, scientific papers analysis, and English proficiency. More sophisticated writing skills, to achieve more comprehensive writing tasks, will be introduced to support students meet the more stringent assessment demands required at levels 5 and 6. The module is well integrated with other technical modules, and ensures students gain foundational competencies for academic and professional development in parallel. Delivered across two semesters, it includes Academic Skills lectures, workshops, and English Support Tutorials.

This module builds on the skills introduced in year 1 and focuses on developing scientific writing, critical thinking skills, scientific papers analysis, and English proficiency. More sophisticated writing skills, to achieve more comprehensive writing tasks, will be introduced to support students meet the more stringent assessment demands required at levels 5 and 6. The module is well integrated with other technical modules, and ensures students gain foundational competencies for academic and professional development in parallel. Delivered across two semesters, it includes Academic Skills lectures, workshops, and English Support Tutorials.

The Essential Medical Biochemistry module covers biomolecule structure/function, enzyme kinetics, and metabolic pathways (e.g., glucose, lipid, amino acid metabolism). It emphasizes biochemical processes in health and disease, linking to precision medicine through pharmacogenomics, biomarker discovery, and metabolic regulation. Topics include bioenergetics, nutrient metabolism, and oxidative stress, with applications in personalized therapies, diagnostics, and understanding genetic influences on biochemical pathways for tailored medical interventions.

Starting with an overview of the genetic material, genome and the genome project, in this module students will get an understanding of the basic principles of molecular biology and its application to understanding genetically linked medical conditions. Students will learn key process of cell life, including gene expression - transcription, RNA processing/editing and translation, and will understand how RNA interference, editing and gene therapy can be used as treatments of medical disorders.

Pathogens pose an increasing threat to human health, and emerging pathogens may cause pandemics which are difficult to prevent and control, as it recently happened for the SARS-CoV2 virus. In addition to infectious diseases, the role of pathogen as co-factors in cancer is becoming increasingly evident. In this module, students will get an understanding of pathogen biology, mechanisms of infection, transmission and prevention of diseases. Students will learn what pathogen-encoded products can be used as diagnostic and therapeutic targets.

This module will provide an overview of pathogenetic mechanisms underlying diseases and how the identification of targets for therapy opens the way for drug design and application. In this module, students will learn basic concepts in pathobiology, including aetiology, pathogenesis and the overall progression of diseases. They will also get an understanding of the basic principles of pharmacology, focussing on how therapeutic drugs can be administered, and how the human body absorbs, distributes, metabolises and excretes pharmaceutical drugs.

The module covers fundamental concepts and methods behind artificial intelligence (AI) and will provide students with the ability to apply the techniques in AI for solving real biomedical data problems. Students will become familiar with the basic principles of machine learning, reasoning and decision making, knowledge representation and inference, etc. AI applications in terms of organising biomedical data, data automation and inference will be explored. The ethical use of AI will be stressed and referenced to medical ethics teaching.

The module introduces the basics of a biological sensor and the variety of sensors in common use in clinical and non-clinical settings. Different sensors for taking measurement lead to the detection of a variety of type of signal and noise as well as a varied source of errors. The underlying physics and chemical principles of different sensors in routine use is discussed, and the challenges of sampling and continuous monitoring is presented. Throughout the module, reference is made to the practical use of medical sensors and how the data scientist is able to best analyse these data.

The module introduces the concepts of probability theory as a mathematical-based tool for looking at randomness and uncertainty of events (or data) in addressing a hypothesis. In order to update probability theory, Bayesian analysis is discussed as a statistical approach to evaluate the probability of the hypothesis with the input of additional new data. The module introduces a number of statistical methods using frequency as an indicator of probability for inference. Subsequently students learn Bayesian analysis to combine statistical inference and prediction that can be used for different problems, and the difference in the approaches highlighted. A number of real-world problems in biomedical and clinical sciences will be discussed illustrating the use of Bayesian analysis in research and clinical decision making.

The module will provide a concise introduction to the fundamental issues of neurobiology, beginning with basic cellular electrophysiology and synaptic transmission and basic networks. A cellular explanation of the organisation of the nervous system together with the functional subdivision into different pathways. . Knowledge of the neuroanatomical architecture will include the peripheral and central nervous system with particular emphasis on the functional partition of the brain. The normal and ageing nervous system will be considered with particular emphasis on neurological diseases, with consideration of the latest research to understand the basis of disease, latest developments in earliest diagnosis and ongoing development of possible treatments.

Clinical chemistry diagnostics involves the measurement of biochemical markers as a key element in the assessment of the function and dysfunction of systems, organs and tissues used by both clinicians and biomedical scientists. In order to successfully diagnose your patient, a variety of samples are taken and analysed in clinical practice that are critical not only for diagnosis, but also central for monitoring subsequent treatment. The module will introduce the student to the nature of samples taken and the initial interpretation of aberrant and normal values.

The module introduces students to key developments in precision medicine, including nanotechnology, immunotherapy, bioinformatics, and structural biology, which are transforming treatment strategies from disease-level to patient-specific approaches. It explores the use of nanoparticles in medicine and the role of genomic sequencing in predicting drug response and tailoring treatments, highlighting the core principles of precision medicine.

This project introduces students to extended projects where they will work individually mastering the use of different instruments. Projects will be variable and project time will be sufficient to enable repetition of experiments and diagnostic tests. This module provides students with transferable skills in teamworking, and communication skills (oral and written) and project work in clinical science projects. Students will be engaged in investigative laboratory project work, and will prepare written research work, maintain a laboratory record book and deliver a presentation to defend against experts.

The aim of the course is to provide a broad understanding of how -omics technologies can be used in a diagnostic setting. Students will learn different types of -omics (e.g. genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics), and how their application in healthcare (cancer, genetic and infectious diseases) can be used to improve diagnostics and therapy. During this course students will learn how different types of biomarkers can be identified and analysed through these technologies, focussing on their application in clinical settings.

Scientific reporting needs to take into account the scientific background of your audience. The module will explain how to appropriately deliver reporting the outcome of a clinical research paper, explaining test results and diagnosis to different stakeholders, including fellow colleagues in your team, clinical colleagues to senior consultants, or to patients, parents and to those with little to no technical background. The module will emphasise development of communication of reports that need to be concise, accurate but prioritise the salient elements of the information that is conveyed. This module addresses scientific reporting through a variety of formats, written, oral and by video.

This module introduces students to extended projects where they will work individually and in teams on carrying out a biomedical or biological data science project. Selecting from a variety of big data sets, different student groups will focus on one set and will identify and develop biomedical/biological problems to frame and resolve using the data science skills acquired to date. This module provides students with transferable skills in teamworking, and communication skills (oral and written) and carrying out project work.

Bioinformatics is a branch of biomedical data science that focuses on the analysis of large volumes of biological and biomedical data (big data) taken from myriad experiments in medical research and clinical diagnostics. The module will discuss examples contemporary of large-scale data sets and the biological inferences that can be derived and will also help the student learn to integrate the fundamental science together with the methods and advanced applications that are being discussed at level 6. This will enable students to become familiar and adept with the specific application of data science to biomedical data sets, to understand and predict change in biological systems, e.g. following treatment, together with a broad understanding and ability to pose fundamental questions themselves.

This module is a branch of machine learning. The module introduces and reinforces the concept artificial neural networks with multiple layers. Students learn that the use of deep learning is of particular use in complex and significant amounts of unstructured data. The principle of layering into neural networks permits more refined pattern recognition to be achieved than regular machine learning and applications of using deep learning techniques in medical data for diagnosis will be presented and discussed.

The module covers the general topic of Digital Signal Processing (DSP) and introduces students the concept of transforming analog and other data to digital data. The range of commonly used mathematical tools used to analyse signal are presented and how patterns and trends can be identified and how it may be used to improve signal quality.

The theory and practice of machine learning is the overarching theme for this module and will include both theoretical and practical aspects of machine learning. The theoretical concepts behind linear and nonlinear regression problems will be discussed and the practical implementation of logistic regression in Python. A variety of techniques used in supervised and unsupervised machine learning will be covered such as linear regression, polynomial regression, classification with logistic regression and clustering. Pattern recognition and its role in machine learning will be introduced together algorithims for its use.

This should allow students to prepare a machine learning approach to a particular problem, identify the appropriate numerical method and implement the algorithm in python. Students should be able to assess the overall performance of this approach.

The data scientist is required to analyse and process data of different nature. Signals represent temporal data, i.e. measurements that change over time. This module takes a deep dive into signals and how systems can be developed to process signals and extract valuable information from them. This module categorises signals into different families and describes their main properties. Techniques to analyse signals in the time and frequency domain are presented. Finally, processing systems that transform signals and extract meaningful features are studied. Computer-based visualisation techniques are used throughout the module to represent abstract mathematical concepts.

This module will mirror the 20-credit SNU314 Pathology module delivered in Nanchang, but is specifically designed for year 3 Nanchang JP students who are completing the final year of their undergraduate degree in London. The module aims to provide an understanding of basic pathological processes with an overview of both non‐neoplastic and neoplastic diseases. Starting from an overview of basic pathological mechanisms including cell injury, wound healing, inflammation and cell adaptations, the module will then introduce classification of diseases based on aetiology, including developmental, inflammatory, degenerative and neoplastic diseases. Students will learn the difference between benign and malignant neoplastic processes, and will learn how to classify, grade, and stage different cancers. The haematology component of this module will provide an understanding of haematopoiesis and haemostasis, and outline the major non‐neoplastic (e.g. genetic and acquired anaemias, coagulopathies) and neoplastic haematological disorders (e.g. tumours deriving from lymphoid, myeloid and histiocytic cells). The module will also provide an overview of non-neoplastic disorders of other systems and organs (e.g. GI, cardiovascular, respiratory system), with minor hints at neoplastic malignancies, which will then be taught by the Cancer Biology module in Sem B.

This module integrates mathematical principles with medical statistics to provide students with a robust foundation for analysing and interpreting medical data. It covers essential concepts, methods, and tools used in the medical field for research, clinical trials and healthcare decision-making. Students will learn how to apply mathematical models and statistical techniques to solve real-world medical problems, ensuring accurate and reliable conclusions from routine testing through to medical research.

This module provides students with a comprehensive framework of basic knowledge in computer science. The course content covers the basic introduction of computer hardware, software, operating system, network, algorithm, data structure, database, programming language and other fields, which lays a foundation for students to further study.

Histology concerns the study of the microstructure and ultrastructure of normal human body under the light microscope and electron microscope, respectively. The relationship between the structure and the function are also elucidated. The content consists of the basic tissues (such as nervous tissue, muscular tissue, epithelial tissue )and organ systems (such as digestive system, respiratory system, blood and vascular system, urinary system,nervous system,motor system, endocrine system and reproductive system). Through the study of this module, students can master the basic theories, knowledges and skills of human histology, laying a solid foundation for learning other modules on basic medical sciences. The module also addresses the microscopic identification of cellular dysfunction, using a selection of common and frequently occurring diseases to illustrate general principles in the universal mechanisms in common pathological processes, when they can be detected at a cellular level.

The module studies the normal morphological structure of the human body and serves as a fundamental and important module in precision medical science. The teaching arrangement of Human Anatomy consists of two parts: theoretical instruction and experimental operation, with the latter being the focus. This module covers both regional and systemic anatomy.

Medical physics is an important branch of physics, which is an independent course formed by combining the principles and methods of physics with medical practice such as prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and healthcare of human diseases. it is an important learning foundation for higher medical and pharmaceutical majors and similar majors.

The concept of a module on systems-based physiology and anatomy introduces the student to an introduction of the concept of biological system and some basic rules of body's functions and anatomical organisation. The basic function of cells is introduced with emphasis on the nature and function of excitable cells and muscle cells to put physiological processes into cellular context. Subsequently an overview of the structure, function and regulation of different organ systems, such as digestive system, respiratory system, blood and vascular system, urinary system, nervous system, motor system, endocrine system and reproductive system is carried out to give the student a fundamental grounding in human anatomy and physiology and their integration.

Advanced Mathematics 1 is a compulsory and fundamental theoretical course for undergraduate students at Biomedical Data Science major. The main content of this course includes and introduction to single-variable and multivariate calculus, series, and elementary ordinary differential equations, among others mathematical approaches.

This module primarily consists of four parts: Set Theory, Mathematical Logic, Graph Theory, and Counting Methods. Set Theory is the branch of mathematics’ that looks at sets and serves as the foundation for the entirety of mathematics and underpins computer science. Mathematical Logic primarily focuses on formalised reasoning systems, thereby training and enhancing logical thinking abilities. Graph Theory represents a practical application of relations and functions between different elements. Counting Methods, on the other hand, is central to techniques for counting the number of elements within series of discrete systems, which greatly aids in understanding the properties of these discrete structures and systems.

The main principles and fundamentals of computer programming will be introduced. The module introduces the data science student to a variety of languages commonly used in programming. Students will learn the main principles of the following languages: Java and C. Given the variety and growth of languages over time, what factors to take into account when choosing one language over another is discussed, and the students will also have opportunity to practically use Java and C programming languages.

Pharmaceutical chemistry is a core foundation discipline in pharmaceutics where the aim is to discover and/or invent and synthesise new chemicals as drugs for treatment. In this module, the student will be introduced to the chemical structure of drugs and their physical and chemical properties and how this relates to stability of medicine in vitro. This primer then leads on to understanding drug action by studying laws of interaction between drug molecules and biological macromolecules. The module concludes with consideration of drugs biological effects, toxicological effects and biological transformation in vivo.

The concept of the Physiology & Pathophysiology progresses at this level to an introduction of the concept of biological systems and some basic rules of body's function, the basic function of cells is introduce, especially the nature and function of excitable cells and muscle cells. And then following the function and regulation of different organ systems, such as digestive system, respiratory system, blood and vascular system, urinary system, nervous system, motor system, endocrine system, energy metabolism and reproductive system. The mechanisms of functional and metabolic changes during the occurrence and development of common and frequently occurring diseases are illustrated after the introduction of general principles in the universal mechanisms in common pathological processes.

Linear algebra is a compulsory mathematical foundation course for undergraduate students major in science, data science and many other disciplines where mathematics is required. The module mainly discusses the theory of finite dimensional linear spaces and introduces the student into strong abstraction and logic. The teaching content mainly includes theoretical knowledge related to determinants, vectors, matrices, systems of linear equations, quadratic forms and related applications.

This module takes typical examples from fields such as physics, ecology, environment, medicine, management, economics, and information technology as its backdrop to elucidate the basic methods and skills of how to establish mathematical models to study and solve practical problems, The purpose of offering this course is not only to impact knowledge but also to cultivate and enhance student's self-learning abilities and innovative qualities through the analysis of typical modelling examples and participation in modelling practical activities.

This module is a fundamental course for computing-related majors, aimed at teaching students how to effectively organise theoretical and physical structures of data, as well as how to design and analyse algorithms to solve practical problems, The course content covers basic data structures (such as arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, trees, graphs, etc,) and algorithm design techniques (such as sorting, searching, recursion, dynamic programming, greedy algorithms, divide-and-conquer, etc., along with the analysis of time and space complexity of algorithms.

This module represents an innovative course that integrates the essence of Medical Statistics and Epidemiology, aiming to construct a comprehensive and in-depth knowledge system to address the complex challenges in the fields of public health and clinical medicine in the 21st century. lt is designed to cultivate public health professionals with solid theoretical foundations and practical abilities. By applying statistical principles and methods to the exploration of disease and health issues, this module serves as an indispensable cornerstone for making sense of clinical and research data of populations and provides a scientific basis for public health decision-making or predictions. The module emphasises the bridging role of statistics in medical practice, akin to a study bridge connecting the vast ocean of data to the shore of health, earning it the reputation of being the "pillar of wisdom in the field of health”.

This module serves as the practical component of data science-related theoretical courses, aiming to comprehensively enhance student's data analysis capabilities through a review of fundamental data science concepts, in-depth learning of data analysis tools and techniques, practical case analysis, and preparation for group projects. Students will master the use of Python data analysis libraries such as Pandas and NumPy, become familiar with data cleaning, transformation, and visualisation techniques and have an initial exposure to machine learning algorithms. Through in-depth analysis of relevant datasets, students will gain insights into the entire process of data analysis, including problem definition, data pre-processing, analysis, visualisation, and interpretation of results. Additionally, the course will guide students in selecting topics for group projects, planning and time management, clarifying team collaboration and division of labour, as well as establishing expected outcomes and evaluation criteria.

The module is one of the backbone of professional courses of medical tests. lt presents to students the basic theory behind the biochemical pathological changes and changes in the quality and quantity of metabolites of disease state on the basis of the body's normal biochemical metabolism, and provides information and decision-making for the diagnosis of the disease, efficacy, prognosis, disease prevention. Through the course students will learn to master the methodology of a variety of clinical biochemistry determinations, the working principles and the use of automatic biochemical analyzers and other common equipment used in clinical biochemistry.

Clinical trials represent the culmination of years of published research leading to consideration towards taking some application into the clinic. This module introduces the student to the detection methods, principles, precautions and methodological evaluation of clinical trials common clinical test items recorded in a trial. Module content introduces the student to different testing regimes that may apply to clinical trials. These include clinical biochemistry test projects, clinical microbiology test projects, clinical immunology test projects and clinical molecular biology test projects

This module introduces the fundamentals of data science, in-depth study of data analysis tools and techniques, practical case studies as small teams in group projects. Through in-depth analysis of relevant data sets, students will complete the whole process data of analysis of biomedical data in a working environment in clinical and allied health and public health problems. This will include students engagement in problem definition, data pre-processing, analysis, visualization, and interpretation of results

The internship modules of graduate practice represents a critical element of the laboratory medicine and precision medical sciences major. During the internship, students will rotate across the various clinical laboratories in the affiliated hospitals to experience the detailed application of their studies in the day-to-day execution of clinical diagnostic tests. This routine work experience will allow students to identify future specialisation as to which type of laboratory(ies) they will target for future employment. It will allow students to reflect and further develop their practical skills and become competent and ready for embarking on work after graduation.

The quality control and Management of the clinical laboratory is a professional core course established to meet the requirements of current clinical laboratory development and management needs. It progresses from the concept of medical laboratories and their management and composition of personnel and roles. Then laboratory management of sample through to data is explored, laboratory layout and safety and integrity, laboratory information and digitisation of data processing and storage, instruments and apparatus for sample analysis and data acquisition and their limitations. Finally a comprehensive understanding of the full process quality management and quality assurance is essential to provide confidence in test data.

Laboratory safety management is very critical issue in college, universities and hospital laboratory settings, which must be in place to prevent accidents or loss of lives or property to oneself or others. The participants and implementers of laboratory activities must have sound personal responsibility, a deep knowledge of safety procedures, and contingency skills to eliminate or reduce the hazards in daily work. This will reduce the occurrence of accidents, and to improve the skill to deal with the accident reasonably and responsibly and to keep away from risk. The module covers such aspects as general knowledge and technology about university laboratory safety, professional safety knowledge in scientific laboratories.

This module is a conjoined study package, which combines the basic theoretical principles together with techniques of microbiological examination of infectious diseases as commonly found in man. Thus a necessary grasp of the basic theory, technical skill and in addition techniques used to identify clinical microbes and microbiological examination is required. lt also introduces students to the concept and over-riding importance of quality control in a clinical diagnostic setting.

This module covers the fundamentals and clinical applications of pharmacology. The basic section includes pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetics, explaining drug mechanisms of action, dose-effect relationships, and processes in the body. It then delves into system-specific drugs, such as those for the nervous system(sedative, hypnotics etc), cardiovascular system and endocrine system. The course also covers chemotherapy drugs and natural medicines. Through theoretical lectures, case analysis, experimental teaching, students will master the pharmacological effects, clinical use and precaution of drugs.

This module primarily focuses on the application of clinical laboratory test results in disease diagnosis. The module provides a bridge between the major of data science to ground the student on the importance of biomedical and clinical data and their use in diagnosis and outcomes of patient or research data. The content covers general clinical test results and disease diagnosis, clinical haematological test results and disease diagnosis, clinical biochemical test results and disease diagnosis, clinical immunology test results and disease diagnosis, clinical microbiology test results and disease diagnosis, clinical molecular biology test results and disease diagnosis, among others.

This module is a core course for computer and data science majors, which mainly describes the basic concepts of digital image processing algorithms. The course content includes basic knowledge of digital image, gray transformation and spatial filtering, frequency domain filtering, image restoration and reconstruction, colour image segmentation, representation and description, and target recognition.

This course will focus on the organisation and interactions of human tissues and their roles in physiology and morphology. It will involve detailed instruction on the appearance, nature and structure of different cell and tissue types, the structure of different organs and the structure-function relationship of tissues within major organs. Topics will include the epithelium and connective tissue, bone, cartilage, blood and muscle tissue, nerve tissue and the nervous system, the circulatory, respiratory, urinary, endocrine, and immune systems, sense organs, skin, digestive tract and glands, male and female reproductive systems.

A general knowledge of normal Human anatomy is essential for the medical student to understand how the
normal body condition relates to aberrant human anatomy throughout different stages of life. Human
anatomy will introduce a functional and regional understanding of human anatomy and the relationships
between organs and systems and how these are affected in disease. Further, this module also underpins
clinical anatomy, and is needed for an effective clinical examination to permit the practicing doctor for first
line diagnosis.

This module follows in the footsteps of Advanced mathematics #1 and serves as a fundamental course for the Biomedical Data sciences major, aiming to provide students with a solid foundation in mathematical theory and tools, enabling them to better understand and data science analytical protocols to biomedical data. The course content extends the use of multivariate calculus, series, ordinary differential equations , and other topics, with an emphasis on integrating mathematical knowledge with practical problems in the field of biomedical data sciences.

This module is intended for students studying BSc Psychology. This module is structured around three main key areas:
(1) Acquiring Essential Skills for Academic Psychology. Through means of lectures and regular tutorials, the module will support you in acquiring a variety of key skills such as experimental report and essay writing, data and information handling, oral and written communication skills and appropriate use of referencing and citations in psychology. You will also be introduced to the critical evaluation skills that will be necessary for your success during further study.
(2) Considering the role of Psychology in the 'real world'. Through class activities and a series of talks from professional Psychologists, you will be encouraged to consider the role of psychology in an applied context and gain a more global perspective of your discipline.
(3) Exploring Career Pathways. You will be given an opportunity to explore various career choices, to reflect on your own career aspirations and to meet with professional Psychologists.

This module is intended for students studying BSc Psychology. This module introduces students to data analysis and statistics in Psychology. Students will learn basic principles of numeracy, data management, probability theory, descriptive statistics and inferential statistics using real-world examples of psychology research. The course will combine lectures and practical sessions including computerised statistical analysis using SPSS.

This module introduces you to experimental design in Psychology. You will understand and critically appraise the different research methods commonly using in psychology research and understand issues critical to experimental design such as sampling, validity, and reliability. Through interactive lectures and practical small-group sessions, you will learn how to select the best experimental design from a range of methods to answer a research question.

This module is intended for students studying BSc Psychology (C800). This module introduces fundamental skills in experimental design, statistical analysis and other methodologies necessary for conducting research in psychology. The module will combine lectures and practical sessions including hand calculation and computerised statistical analysis using SPSS.

This module aims to provide you as psychology students with a scientific overview of biology, emphasizing concepts relevant to behaviour and its study. This supports the distinctiveness of QMUL psychology as a natural and experimental science and introduces students to the growing notion of psychology as a branch of the biological sciences (e.g., that "behaviour" is the end product of whole organism biology).
It will also introduce you to the integrative scientific thinking skills required to study subsequent psychological topics. You will be introduced to empirical findings and will critically evaluate the range of methods in the field.
Topics covered include basic cell biology, genetics, cell signaling, development, and principles of evolution as related to behaviour.

This module introduces themes at Level 4 in psychology and considers a unique area of psychological research: Positive Psychology which focuses on psychological well-being and optimal functioning as well as the individual and social determinants thereof. The aim is to introduce this field of psychology and explore its relationship to other areas of psychology. Key studies, and their ethical dimensions, from both classic and modern biological, experimental and intervention perspectives are provided throughout.

This module is intended for students studying BSc Psychology (C800). This module builds on the theme of psychology as a biological science in parallel with the 'Exploring Psychology' module by specifying the proximate biological mechanisms involved in psychological phenomena. The module will focus on basic principles of biological psychology predominantly, and then introduce psychological processes to illustrate these.

This module introduces and develops basic concepts in the philosophy of science and its relevance to psychology as a discipline. A biological framework for psychological science is also provided. It then introduces basic cognitive science/psychology, social psychology, differential psychology and an introduction to brain and behaviour relationships.

This module builds upon PSY124 Exploring Psychology I by extending the introduction of basic concepts, theories, methods and research findings in psychology. The areas introduced include the core and interdisciplinary fields in psychology. Lectures for exploring psychology II will include an introductory lecture followed by lectures on specific topics in psychology.

The module will allow you to learn about the different conceptualisations of emotion both in terms of historical developments as well as contemporary theoretical models of emotions. The module will also consider the biological basis of emotions in the brain and the body, how emotions are expressed and perceived in faces, bodies, voice and music. The relationship between emotions and cognitions will be considered, including emotion regulation and individual differences in emotions. Finally, cultural differences and disorders of emotion will be discussed.

This module builds introduces an area of special interest to applied psychologists, and one where the College has research strengths; health psychology or psychology as applied to health and medicine. The module covers the central models and evidence base concerning the relationship of psychological processes to health maintenance, treatment adherence, professional-patient interactions, stress and immune system function. Topics covered by this module include models and theories of health behaviour and their explanatory power; psychology & health promotion; adherence to treatment, health professional and patient interactions; research methods in health psychology; psychological issues in clinical trial design; personality, health and lifestyle; psychoneuroimmunology; cardiovascular disease; sexual health behaviours; and coping with chronic & terminal conditions.

This module builds introduces an area of special interest to applied psychologists, and one where the College has research strengths; health psychology or psychology as applied to health and medicine. The module covers the central models and evidence base concerning the relationship of psychological processes to health maintenance, treatment adherence, professional-patient interactions, stress and immune system function. Topics covered by this module include models and theories of health behaviour and their explanatory power; psychology & health promotion; adherence to treatment, health professional and patient interactions; research methods in health psychology; psychological issues in clinical trial design; personality, health and lifestyle; psychoneuroimmunology; cardiovascular disease; sexual health behaviours; and coping with chronic & terminal conditions.

This module is intended for students studying BSc Psychology (C800) and its variants. This module introduces you to qualitative research methods in Psychology. You will understand and critically appraise the different qualitative research methods commonly used in psychology research and understand issues critical to research design and analysis such as data collection protocols, sampling, and researcher positionality. Through interactive lectures and practical sessions, you will learn how to select the best data collection protocol from a range of methods to answer a research question.

This module is only available to students who enter under the C1C8 programme. This module builds upon themes developed in level 4 psychology modules and considers specific cognitive functions and properties of the human mind. The material covered will include traditional cognitive psychology, cognitive neuroscience and cognitive neuropsychology (the understanding of normal cognitive processes through unique case studies of human brain damage). Cognitive functions examined will include visual, object and spatial perception, psychophysics, memory processes, complex reasoning, language, face processing and the relationship between emotion and these processes. Experiments and studies from classical and modern cognitive psychology will be provided throughout.

Have you ever wondered what influences our perceptions, emotions, thoughts, and behaviours? This module in Social Psychology will provide an overview of the classic and contemporary scientific theories and methods used to address how other people and different contexts can shape these processes. Topics covered will include the self, social cognition, attitudes and attitude change, social influence, group processes, and stereotyping, prejudice and discrimination.

This module surveys developmental psychology, covering human development across the whole life span but with a more detailed focus on development in the early years (infancy/childhood). The aim of the module is to introduce the key questions, theories, concepts, methodology, studies and research findings within developmental psychology, regarding different domains of psychological functioning including social, emotional, cognitive, and behavioural development. The module will also cover the prenatal period, physical, motor, and sensory development, learning theory, moral development, and development of the self (identity).

This module provides an in-depth analysis of a central area of psychology known variously as "individual differences" or "differential psychology". We will build on several key areas of psychology introduced in previous modules that show substantial individual differences including personality, psychopathology, intelligence and cognition. We will then explore the proposed causes and effects of these individual differences drawing from research using approaches from psycho-dynamics to behavioral genetics. Finally, we will explore the evidence behind several key controversies in individual differences including the continuum between personality and mental heath, the nature vs nurture debate, race differences in intelligence and genetic determinism.

As for other species, many abilities and behaviours that we take for granted - from perception to learning, communication, handedness and sexual preferences - are the result of our evolutionary history. Our history has shaped our psychology and influences our daily behaviour. Are we the only species that is deceived by visual illusions? Who is the most intelligent species? Are we the only ones that exhibit handedness? Which are the mechanisms of learning? To understand what makes as human, we have to look at ourselves from a broader perspective. In this module we will explore differences and similarities between humans beings and other species. We will learn how to access and compare the mind and behaviour of individuals that do not possess language such as human neonates, newly-hatched chicks and other models currently used in understanding of healthy and pathological behaviour.

This module is designed to give you a scientific overview of psychopathology based on related theoretical frameworks and empirical findings, and to critically evaluate the range of approaches in this field. In this course, you will focus on the history of the classification and diagnosis of common mental health disorders, and on key common mental disorders including mood disorders (depression & bipolar disorder), anxiety disorders and schizophrenia. Psychological therapies will also be discussed. You will develop an understanding of the symptoms and diagnoses across the mental disorders as well as the risk factors and treatments used for common mental disorders.

This module introduces you to the fundamental concepts in the psychological study of online behaviour, the psychological processes associated with human interactions with the Internet and emerging technologies, as well as the application of this knowledge in a wide variety of sectors.
Studying and understanding human behaviour in relation to technology is vital, as people interact with cyberspace more and more everyday. Therefore, understanding the application of psychology in modern practices, for example why people behave differently when they go online than they do in real life, displaying different personalities in cyberspace is important. This module will build upon your existing knowledge from modules in the BSc Psychology curricumum, such as Social Psychology and Individual Differences. It will include topics such as: the presentation of the self online, the relationship between personality and behaviour online, romance online, as well as the psychological impact of certain behaviours online leading to victimisation and internet addiction. In addition, research will be explored on artificial psychology and the role of ethics in human-computer interaction.

Taking a multi-disciplinary approach, this module will provide students with an in-depth understanding of different theoretical conceptualizations of creativity, how it can be measured empirically and the extent to which this research can inform practices in areas such as education, business and mental health. It will draw on research from various different disciplines within psychology, covering areas such as neuroscience, social, developmental and cognitive psychology and creative arts. By exploring evolutionary foundations and creativity research in non-humans, cognitive processes underlying creativity and creativity as a strategy for fostering resiliency it will also highlight links to key focal areas and research strengths within the School of Psychology.

This module introduces you to the fundamental concepts in the psychological study of crime. The areas
introduced include: the forensic psychologist, the study of crime, psychological explanations of crime, psychological explanations of the criminal mind, psychological explanations of specific crime types (for example, crimes of a sexual nature), the role of criminal and forensic psychologists in detection and investigation, and psychology in prison.

This module explores current topics in mental health from both historical and contemporary perspectives. It includes in-depth analyses of contemporary issues in the field, such as the social/biological/cultural influences to mental health, the diagnosis and treatment of mental disorders, and/or the role of public policy in mental health diagnosis and treatment. Key themes may include studying mental health across multiple levels of analysis (from cellular to cultural), and how our understanding of mental health has evolved over time. This module aims to advance critical reasoning skills through the analysis of empirical research, debates in the literature, and the discussion of the broader socio-cultural context of the mental health sciences.

The workplace is a dynamic place, constantly changing, evolving and adapting in the face of global changes in new technologies, new ways of working and changing social, economical and political norms. In order to keep a workplace running like a fine tuned machine, it often takes the efforts of many individuals. In many ways, this is where organizational psychology comes in place, which is the branch of psychology studying the workplace environment in all its liveness by promoting effective practices to maximize the benefits for both the organizations and their employees. In this module, you will be introduced in key issues in organizational psychology and how they apply in the workplace. Topics will include employee selection and training, team-work, leadership, fairness and well-being in the workplace, and organizational change and development.

Decision-making is embedded in every action we take, from the most basic (e.g. whether or not to his Snooze on our alarm) to some of the most important (e.g. what partner we end up being with, what house we buy, what career we pursue). This lecture and seminar based module is designed to expose students to core theoretical and empirical work on decision-making and how it has been applied to address current public policy issues (e.g., sustainable consumption, healthy eating, weight reduction, debt reduction). Each week the module will present theoretical and empirical work on decision-making to understand how we make personal, social and moral decisions and through a seminar based approach will facilitate debate on how this work has been applied, through case examples of actual public policy, to support behavioural change. This combination of basic and applied psychology is framed around understanding core psychological processes that underpin decision-making (e.g. agency, control, causal inference) in order to critically evaluate where psychology can best contribute to addressing real world policy issues.

The aim of this module is to give students a thorough understanding of the theoretical approaches in cognitive and affective neuroscience, where we will evaluate evidence from both behavioural and neuropsychological studies. We will explore how normal cognitive functioning takes place and how this can be elucidated by looking at brain damaged patients and neuroimaging studies. The lecture series will include an introductory lecture on the overall aims and objectives of cognitive neuroscience followed by a series of lectures looking at attention, perception, memory and movement. Subsequent lectures will focus on affective neuroscience, looking at neuroscience of empathy; neural basis of emotional reactivity, including attentional processes, biases and emotion regulation; and neuroscience of different emotions such as fear, anger, or disgust.

This module introduces cognitive behavioural therapies (CBT) and their use across healthcare settings. CBT is the mostresearched form of psychotherapy, and the recommended psychological intervention for most mental health symptoms.
Students will learn how CBT is applied in understanding psychological problems, by examining the evidence-based cognitive behavioural models for different mental health conditions, such as mood disorders, anxiety disorders, obsessive compulsive and trauma disorders. You will be introduced to the theory and the practice of 'doing CBT', critically examining a broad range of therapeutic skills and treatment protocols for addressing specific disorders. Case studies will be used throughout to promote the
translation of theoretical knowledge into practical applications and vice versa, and to achieve in-depth understanding.

In this module, we will address the concept of vulnerability within three contexts: (1) Humanitarian, focusing on war affected children/youth groups and forcibly displaced families, (2) Educational, focusing on students with mental health risks and their families, (3) Workplace, focusing on minority employees. We will discuss theoretical perspectives around vulnerability, case studies outlining the factors shaping vulnerability and the needs of vulnerable groups, and the current trends in psychological practice and policies to support those groups.
This module builds on themes developed in level 4 and 5 psychology modules. It will consider areas of psychology which are the subject of active research in the SBBS Department of Psychology.

Climate change, plastic pollution, biodiversity loss and other environmental problems cause feelings of helplessness to many. In the Environmental Psychology module, you will explore psychological factors that determine pro-environmental choices and learn about the most effective means to facilitate sustainable behaviour. The module will also cover how natural environments affect humans and how to deal with eco-anxiety. You will carry out a practical project on campus or nearby businesses to develop applied psychology skills.

This module provides an in-depth analysis of a new, rapidly evolving, and often controversial area, of psychology and psychiatry. We will build on several key areas of psychology introduced in previous modules including social, biological and abnormal psychology to explore how genetic and environmental factors come together to cause mental illnesses such as major depression, schizophrenia and autism. Drawing on the most recent research from quantitative and molecular genetics we will explore the evidence behind several key controversies in the field including the continuum between traits and disorders, the nature vs nurture debate, genetic determinism and the ethical implications of genetic research of mental illness.

This module introduces students to the professional field of Sport and Exercise Psychology. It will address the psychological techniques used for improving athletic performance, team cohesion, athlete wellbeing, etc., and the psychological benefits and risks associated with exercise.
The content builds on your previous knowledge about cognitive, clinical and health psychology, and applies this knowledge to real-life problems in the form of case studies.
You will build a portfolio of case studies, covering various types of problems and intervention techniques.
You will learn how theoretical concepts of cognition, emotion, motivation, attachment and psychological interventions can be applied to real-life problems relating to individual and team sports.

This module will present contemporary research on play in animals, children and adults, focusing on psychological theories, especially during development. The module will also utilise an applied approach to studying how different psychological mechanisms may underlie playing different games, such as board, role-playing and video games, achieved by playing and discussing games in class. You will debate societal issues related to games, such as the role of video games in violence or game addiction, but also the positive effects of games.

This module will provide you with a broad overview of the major childhood and adolescent neurodevelopmental and mental health conditions, including epidemiology and development, risk and protective factors and interventions. You will learn about the current research in childhood and adolescent psychopathology and how to critically appraise the evidence base for interventions. The module will also explore the role of societal changes (e.g., digitalisation, family structure), and broader context (e.g., loneliness, bullying, academic pressure) on adolescent psychological wellbeing and mental health. Finally, you will explore the role of broader psychosocial factors and culture in our understanding of childhood and adolescent psychopathology.

Consciousness is one of the greatest remaining mysteries in all of biology: the ability to experience the world is one of the key considerations of what makes us human. This module will delve into the psychology and neuroscience of consciousness, reflecting the most recent progress in the field. It will explore ethical considerations in the study of consciousness, and consider the implications of diminished consciousness in psychiatric and neurological conditions, such as depression and dementia.

This module allows you to conceive, design and carry out a substantive, original empirical study in an area of psychology independently. You will work on approved research topics set by project supervisors. Experimental or theoretical work is the principal component of the project. The work also involves critical evaluation of data previously published in the literature. A consideration of ethical issues is also required. A dissertation is prepared. This module will teach you to work on original scientific research topics and consolidate quantitative research skills, communication and critical evaluation. It will enhance your understanding of psychology in a broader context and will provide students with experience of working in a research environment.

The extended essay is intended to give you an opportunity to study in-depth a topic of particular interest to you within the subject of Psychology. The essay will not entail you conducting empirical research.
You can choose to do the Extended Essay rather than PSY600 Psychology Research Project but will need to take another 15-credit module in your final year. The Extended Essay module is intended to provide an opportunity for you to write substantively, critically and independently about a selected and approved area of Psychology than is possible in a tutorial essay. The work also involves significant evaluation of theoretical issues relevant to the topic under investigation and you are expected to use original research articles. The assessment comprises a substantive written dissertation.

The module will allow students to learn about the different conceptualisations of emotion both in terms of historical developments as well as contemporary theoretical models of emotions. The module will also consider the biological basis of emotions in the brain and the body, how emotions are expressed and perceived in faces, bodies, voice and music. The relationship between emotions and cognitions will be considered, including emotion regulation and individual differences in emotions. Finally, cultural differences and disorders of emotion will be discussed.

This module introduces theory and research in cognitive psychology, the study of the human mind and mental processes. Key theories and research in cognitive psychology will be discussed, including visual and multi-modal perception, attention, memory, language, reasoning, and decision-making. Experiments and studies from classical and modern cognitive psychology will be provided and discussed critically throughout to illustrate these concepts. This module will demonstrate the essential role of that cognitive psychology plays in everyday life.

This module introduces and critically discusses an area of special interest to applied psychologists, namely, psychology as applied to health behaviour. The course covers the central models and evidence bases concerning the relationship between psychological processes and health and illness. Topics covered by this module will include health promotion and public health; health behaviour models; illness maintenance and treatment adherence; chronic illness; and health through the lifespan.

This module provides an in-depth analysis of a central area of psychology known variously as 'individual differences' or 'differential psychology'. We will build on several key areas of psychology that show substantial individual differences including personality, psychopathology, intelligence and cognition. We will then explore the proposed causes and effects of these individual differences drawing from research using approaches from psycho-dynamics to behavioral genetics. Finally, we will explore the evidence behind several key controversies in individual differences including the continuum between personality and mental health, the nature vs nurture debate, race differences in intelligence and genetic determinism.

Students wishing to take a year abroad are recommended to look at the QMUL Outgoing students information for a list of current partner institutions.

https://www.qmul.ac.uk/international/global-opportunities/outgoing-students/

This module involves and extended placement in a professional workplace and is a core module on the "Year in Industry/Research" programmes in the fields of Biology (incl. Zoology, Medical Genetics), Biochemistry, Biomedical Sciences, Neuroscience, and Psychology offered by SBBS. Students are supported to secure a work placement through a range of employability initiatives that are already in place at SBBS. The placement will normally be 10-12 months in duration and must not be less than 6 months in length. This is accommodated within a BSc programme extended to four years duration.

This module provides an introduction to the fundamentals of medical sciences which may include topics on medicinal chemistry, biochemistry, chemistry of genetics and functional anatomy. Students will be introduced to basic concepts in chemistry such as intermolecular forces, stereochemistry and the relationships between different functional groups in chemical structures of drugs and their activities. Students will also study an introduction on how different molecular structures of drugs can affect their physicochemical properties which subsequently impact on the stability of medicines.

This module provides an introduction to the action of medicinal drugs including an understanding of the basic principles of pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetics. The module will look at major drug classes and examine how drugs elicit their effects by interaction with specific targets and the factors that control (i) how drugs reach those targets; (ii) the duration of action; (iii) individual variation in the response to drugs. Drug treatment of major medical conditions will be discussed, including the rationale for prescribing a particular class of drug(s).

Starting from a brief introduction to the history of microbiology, including different biogenetic and abiogenetic theories, this module will provide an overview of different class of pathogens (e.g. bacteria, viruses, parasites) and related diseases. Students will also learn how to prevent infections and disease, and will learn the fundamentals of epidemiology. During the practical sessions, students will have the opportunity to identify different types of pathogens (e.g. through slide observation, bacterial cultures) and learn laboratory diagnosis and prevention.

Clinical chemistry involves the measurement of biochemical markers as a key element in the assessment of the function and dysfunction of systems, organs and tissues used by both clinicians and biomedical scientists. In order to successfully diagnose your patient, a variety of samples are taken and analysed in clinical practice that are critical not only for diagnosis, but also central for monitoring subsequent treatment. The module will introduce the student to the nature of samples taken and the initial interpretation of aberrant and normal values and how these align with disease, and this challenges the students through multiple possible diagnoses in a hierarchical fashion. Thus, critical analytical skills are highly developed in the module.

The module aims to provide an understanding of basic pathological processes with an overview of both non‐neoplastic and neoplastic diseases. Starting from an overview of basic pathological mechanisms including cell injury, wound healing, inflammation and cell adaptations, the module will then introduce classification of diseases based on aetiology, including developmental, inflammatory, degenerative and neoplastic diseases. Students will learn the difference between benign and malignant neoplastic processes, and will learn how to classify, grade, and stage different cancers. The haematology component of this module will provide an understanding of haematopoiesis and haemostasis, and outline the major non‐neoplastic (e.g. genetic and acquired anaemias, coagulopathies) and neoplastic haematological disorders (e.g. tumours deriving from lymphoid, myeloid and histiocytic cells). The module will also provide an overview of non-neoplastic disorders of other systems and organs (e.g. GI, cardiovascular, respiratory system), with minor hints at neoplastic malignancies, which will then be taught by the Cancer Biology module in Sem B.

This module examines the biological, psychological, and social factors that influence mental health and
mental health conditions. The module provides foundational knowledge of common mental health
conditions, covering symptoms, underlying causes, and evidence-based treatments. In addition, students
will be introduced to experimental methods in psychology and neuroscience to study mental health and
better understand the basis of mental health conditions. Students will learn about the basics of
neuroscientific methods, from research using animal models to neuroimaging. In workshops, students will
gain hands-on experience in analysing and interpreting data of various methods (animal work, EEG,
functional magnetic resonance imaging). A field trip exploring the history of mental health research and
treatment in London is included as part of the summer school.

It is recommended that students taking this module have previously studied introductory-level psychology or are enrolled on an equivalent course. Good numerical and English language skills are essential. A-level equivalent knowledge of psychology or a background in neuroscience is required.

This module examines how marketing can drive social change and sustainability, extending beyond commercial objectives to tackle societal, ethical, and environmental challenges. Topics explored include sustainable marketing and consumer behaviour, corporate social responsibility and ethics, and social marketing and behaviour change strategies, with the aim of developing sustainability and social impact competencies, addressing the green skills gap, and evaluating the impact of social marketing interventions. We focus on these themes to understand their implications for consumer behaviour, business practices, and society at large.

This module explores the dynamic intersections of influencer marketing and artificial intelligence (AI), equipping students with the insights and skills to navigate these critical aspects of modern marketing. Through this module, students will gain an in-depth understanding of influencer culture within both traditional and digital marketing landscapes. Key topics include the role of influencers in digital marketing, strategies for brand-influencer partnerships, online community building, and content creation that resonates across platforms. Students will analyze various types of creative and strategic content, developing the skills to create impactful marketing campaigns.

What does the future world of work look like? This module critically evaluates contemporary trends in the changing world of work. We focus on these trends with a view to understanding their implications for work, employment and society. Some issues explored in this module are: automation and AI; emotional labour; flexible working; the platform economy; climate change; regulation and the role of the state; globalisation. The extent to which COVID-19 has disrupted, or accelerated, such trends will also be explored throughout.

This module introduces students to the core principles of marketing and explores how artificial intelligence is transforming modern marketing practices. Topics include consumer behaviour, segmentation, branding, and marketing strategy, alongside AI applications such as predictive analytics, personalisation, and digital advertising. Through interactive workshops, case studies, and an AI Skills Bootcamp, students will develop practical knowledge and critical understanding of how data-driven technologies are transforming marketing practice.. No prior experience in marketing or AI is required.

This module introduces students to a range of theoretical perspectives relevant to managing equality and diversity in contemporary organisations, and aims to equip them with knowledge and skills to create inclusive workplace environments. The module will first introduce students to various dimensions of diversity like gender, age, race and so on, and explore why inclusion matters and how it relates to business and organisational success. We will then examine a range of theories that help explain how different labour market and organisational processes may produce and reproduce inequalities. The final part of the module will consider the importance of leadership in creating organizational inclusion and explore how to design and deliver effective diversity initiatives in organisations.

The CISI Investment Operations Certificate is one of the benchmark entry-level qualification into the UK investment profession. It delivers the threshold competency knowledge required by investment professionals. Key content areas appropriate for these roles will be covered in this module, such as: financial markets and institutions, ethics, and regulation and legal concepts.

The module aims to support students in getting started on their career journey by introducing key timelines within the employability process, alongside how to create a competitive CV. This includes developing compelling bullet points and becoming familiar with LinkedIn, including what an effective profile looks like. The intention is to enable students to begin applying, explore opportunities of interest, and feel prepared to take the next steps.

The module builds on the Personal and Career Development Plan from year one, continuing to focus on how students can explore career options, acquire experiences to support this and enhance employability. Students are also introduced to activities to help them succeed in competitive recruitment & selection processes.

The aim of the module is to help students grow as individuals by developing a broad range of skills and attributes that, in turn, will enhance their opportunities to secure good careers and further professional and personal development. From the careers point of view, the module places a particular focus on helping students securing graduate level employment. From an academic point of view, the module intends to support students in acquiring greater awareness of postgraduate studies in economics, finance, data analysis and management. From the graduate attributes point of view the module aims at supporting students in extending their understanding through academic enquiry, to use information constructively and critically and to communicate effectively with a range of audiences.

The aim of this module is to introduce the basic concepts and methods that economists employ to analyse economic growth and international trade. It will review and analyse the current macroeconomic issues and events from the perspective of the business community and policymakers, including: strategies for growth; causes of trade deficits; consequences of government deficits; short- and long-term effects of monetary policy; and the globalisation of financial markets. The module will feature examples from both developed and developing countries to enhance knowledge of the world economy and skills in solving practical problems.

The module introduces macroeconomics in a closed economy. It covers the measurement of GDP, inflation and unemployment; long-run equilibrium in goods, labour and financial markets; money, banking and money supply; money demand and money-market equilibrium;
and short-run fluctuations using the Keynesian cross, ISMP and aggregate demand/aggregate supply frameworks. Students analyse how fiscal policy, monetary policy and other shocks affect output, employment, interest rates, inflation and the price level.

This module provides an introduction to the core concepts and analytical frameworks of corporate finance, focusing on financial decision-making within organisations and financial markets.
