The module develops students’ understanding of key financial principles, establishing a foundation for further study in finance at higher levels, while relating financial theory to contemporary business practice and real-world financial decision-making. It also equips students with the analytical and financial literacy skills needed to succeed in a competitive job market.

This module is the first in a sequence of three modules intended to provide students with a thorough introduction to microeconomic theory. This module will cover: introduction to microeconomic modelling; producer theory: technology and costs, competitive supply, monopoly supply; consumer theory: the budget set, preferences and utility, competitive demand, price and income effects, and intertemporal choice.

This module will be an introduction to economic reasoning and analysis. No prior knowledge of economics is necessary. The module will cover concepts and frameworks to understand contemporary issues such as market power, inequality, and climate change

This module provides a detailed introduction to the core mathematical techniques and concepts that are necessary for the study of economics and finance. Topics covered include: linear and non-linear functions; differentiation; constrained and unconstrained optimisation; vectors and matrices.

The module is an introduction to Probability and Statistics. Topics include: Descriptive statistics and linear regression; Probability theory; Random variables and probability distributions; Sampling distributions; Estimation; Confidence intervals; Hypothesis testing. The objective of this module is to give students a grounding in the use of data for description and inference. Topics include descriptive statistics; probability theory; random variables and probability distributions; sampling distributions; properties of estimators; confidence intervals; hypothesis testing.

This module develops practical skills that are essential for success both during your undergraduate studies and in your future career. You will learn how to obtain, analyse, and represent economic and financial data using standard databases and spreadsheet software. You will also learn the principles of effective writing in a professional context, enabling you to use language effectively to communicate your arguments and conclusions. You will understand how data and writing skills are connected.

The CFA Investment Management Certificate (IMC) is one of the benchmark entry-level qualification into the UK investment profession. It delivers the threshold competency knowledge required by investment professionals involved in portfolio management, research analysis, and other front office investment activities. Key content areas appropriate for these roles will be covered in this module, such as: financial markets and institutions, ethics, and regulation and legal concepts.

This module will be an introduction to economic reasoning and analysis. It will provide investment specialists with the relevant micro and macro economic tools needed to understand the functioning of financial markets and institutions and with the relevant understanding of how economic policy impacts financial markets.

The aim of this module is to provide a rigorous introductory training in the theory of investment and capital markets and a good understanding of its central concepts. The module will equip students with sound understanding of the main characteristics of investment instruments and how those instruments can be used to meet investors' objectives.

This module is the first in a sequence of work based modules, which are designed to provide opportunities to engage in structured learning activities in the workplace. The focus of this module is on preparing apprentices to become successful finance professionals. Apprentices will develop their knowledge and skills of the systems and processes required to perform operational duties, including learning how to analyse market data and how to communicate with internal and external clients.

The module covers the principles underlying the working of financial institutions. It introduces the theory and operation of financial systems. Students are expected to gather a sound understanding of the structure of the Financial Services industry and in particular the role and purpose of markets and the process of investing.

This module develops practical skills that are essential for financial professionals. You will learn how to obtain, analyse, and visualise relevant data using standard spreadsheet software. You will also learn key statistical concepts and how to apply them to financial data.

This module is the second in a sequence of two Level 4 work based modules, which are designed to provide opportunities to engage in structured learning activities in the workplace. The focus of this module is on preparing apprentices to become successful finance professionals. Apprentices will develop their knowledge and skills of service delivery, of autonomy in problem solving, as well the ability to coach less experienced colleagues.

This module is part of the foundation of modern macroeconomics. In this module, we study two main topics. The first is growth theory, where we consider both exogeneous and endogenous growth models. The second topic is open economy macroeconomics, where we consider balance of payments, exchange rates and the Mundell-Fleming model.

This course introduces students to international macroeconomics, stressing financial aspects. It covers the balance of payments, the role and determinants of exchange rates, the effect of macroeconomic policies in an open economy, a history of the international monetary system, and an assessment of the consequences of financial globalization

This module studies general equilibrium in competitive markets, market failure, and information economics. You will be shown how to find a set of prices that clear multiple markets simultaneously, both in exchange economies and in economies with production, and you will investigate the welfare properties of such equilibria. You will then analyse the consequences of consumption and production externalities, as well as the provision of public goods. Finally, you will examine the effects of information asymmetries; including adverse selection, moral hazard, and market signalling.

This module provides an introduction to game theory, a framework for studying situations of strategic interdependence. You will be shown how to describe such situations formally, how to analyse them using concepts of dominance and equilibrium, and how the theory can be applied to questions arising in various social sciences. Concepts and techniques to be studied include: games in extensive and strategic form, backward induction, strategic dominance, imperfect information, choice under uncertainty, pure and mixed strategy Nash equilibrium, coordination and outguessing games, the prisoners' dilemma, subgame perfection, iterative dominance, commitment and credibility, and repeated games.

This module builds on students' understanding of statistics to introduce them to the theoretical and practical principles of elementary econometrics. There are three main objectives: to provide a solid grounding in the theory and practice of simple and multiple regression analysis; to introduce students to the key threats to the validity of OLS estimation — including omitted variable bias, functional misspecification, simultaneous causality, sample selection bias, and measurement errors — and to possible solutions, such as instrumental variable methods and randomised controlled trials; and to teach students how to implement these methods on real-world data using the software package R.

This module further develops students' knowledge of econometrics by introducing a variety of concepts and methods used extensively in applied work. Topics to be covered include: nonlinear regression functions, instrumental variables regression, stationary and nonstationary time series, panel data, and binary dependent variables. Implementation of these techniques using the software package R will be an additional focus of the module.

This module recognises and supports a full year of professional experience undertaken as part of a student’s degree programme. The module enables students to apply academic knowledge in a real‑world organisational setting, develop industry relevant skills, and gain insight into professional practices in their chosen field within economics and/or finance. The module emphasises the development of key competencies such as communication, problem‑solving, teamwork, digital literacy, and professional judgement. As part of the assessment, students will deliver a reflective presentation at some point during their placement; outlining their placement experience and demonstrating evidence of skill development. They will also complete monthly journal entries to support ongoing engagement throughout the year’

This course covers the basic theoretical tools to understand what determines international trade (the flow of goods across countries) and international economic relations more generally. Some of the topics covered by the module are: Labor productivity and comparative advantage: the Ricardian model; Resources and Trade: the Heckscher-Ohlin model; External economies of scale and the international location of production; Firms in the global economy: export decisions, outsourcing, and multinational enterprises; The instruments of trade policy; The political economy of trade policy.

The module introduces students to modern, dynamics theories of consumption and saving decisions, fixed investment, unemployment and labour turnover and the business cycle. Further topics include positive theories of fiscal and monetary policy in the medium to long-run and their implications for fiscal sustainability and inflation.

This is a module in the applied microeconomic analysis of social issues of topical importance in and outside the UK. Issues such as crime, poverty, and mental health would seem to be the main research domain of social sciences such as psychology, sociology, and politics. However, economics has provided valuable theoretical and empirical insights that have contributed to current debates on all these issues. Students will have the opportunity to look at these various social issues through the lens of the economic approach.

This module will provide students with the necessary skills to analyse and understand corporate investment and corporate financing choices. Students will understand how investments and financing decisions affect the value of the firm and will be exposed to the analytical tools necessary for evaluating real and financial assets.

This course will offer students understanding of reporting and accounting principles. From basic bookkeeping to the preparation of financial statements and an understanding of the way in which accounts are analysed using accountancy ratios. Students will also learn the basic concepts of accounting and international accounting standards. Students will acquire an understanding of financial statements and of the way in which accounts are analysed using accountancy ratios.

This course will introduce you to how economists analyse the interaction among goods, labour and financial markets. These are the markets in which important variables of interest such as GDP (output), (un)employment, and inflation (price levels), among others, are determined. You will also further develop your understanding of how economic policy impacts financial markets.

Quantitative Methods for Finance 2 will expand your understanding of basic statistical reasoning and of relevant financial concepts. The module explores methods for managing and analysing financial datasets, and will equip you with the key skills that Investment Operations Specialists require, such as the ability to manipulate data using specialised computer software.

This course aims to familiarise students with how the foreign exchange market operates and the key influences on exchange rates. At the end of the course students should understand FX trading and some key FX trading strategies. The course also gives students a background on the impact of economic policy on exchange rates.

This module will introduce students to a variety of empirical methods that are commonly used to estimate the causal effect of a policy change (e.g., an increase in the minimum wage) on economic outcomes (e.g., employment and sales). Techniques to be covered may include: randomised controlled trials, regression analysis, instrumental variables, difference-in-differences, regression-discontinuity design, event studies, synthetic control methods, propensity-score matching, and machine learning. These methods will be illustrated in the context of contemporary issues drawn from fields such as health, labour, and development; bridging the gap between introductory econometrics and elective modules in applied economics.

This module provides an overview of managerial strategy from the perspective of microeconomic principles, with emphasis placed both on conceptual understanding and on application to real-world problems faced by managers. Topics to be covered may include: the boundaries of the firm, specialisation and diversification, economies of scale and scope, the learning curve, make-or-buy decisions, market and industry analysis, pricing decisions, entry and exit decisions, strategic commitment, sources of competitive advantage, five-forces analysis, incentives in organisations, human resource management, performance measurement, and corporate culture.

This module focuses on the three main financial statements issued by companies: the balance sheet, the income statement, and the cash-flow statement. Students will also learn basic accounting concepts and will become familiar with international accounting standards. Topics to be covered include accountancy ratios (e.g., solvency, profitability, and efficiency), double entry bookkeeping, and budgetary planning.

This module offers a rigorous introduction to asset pricing and the theory of capital markets. It examines the investment decisions of households and firms, and studies the behaviour of the financial markets in which these decisions are made. Topics to be covered include: stock valuation, the relationship between risk and return, basic bond analysis, risk aversion, portfolio choice, the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM), arbitrage pricing theory, and empirical evidence on security returns. The module introduces students to programming in Python

This module is organised around two key topics in corporate finance. The first part will focus on the investments made by firms: Students will learn how investment choices affect the value of the firm, and will become familiar with the analytical tools needed for valuation of real and financial assets. The second part of the module will study how firms choose their capital structure, as well as corporate governance mechanisms that can be put in place to improve access to external financing.

This module introduces students to the institutions of modern banking and to the role of banks as financial intermediaries in the economy. Topics discussed will include: the origins and history of banking, the types of banks and the range of products and services they offer, banking supervision and regulation, the functions of a Central Bank, securitisation and financial innovation, shadow banking, and recent changes in intermediation technology. The module has a focus on the institutional details of the banking sector that will inform both further study of finance and potential employment in the financial services industry.

The Big Data for Financial Professionals module will equip students with the empirical techniques to use and analyse large financial datasets. By the end of the course, students will be able to use modern empirical techniques such as machine learning on large financial datasets. Students will learn how to handle real-world data and use econometric software.

This module will provide students with deep understanding of the structure of the investment industry and the functioning of financial markets. As well as an understanding of the impact the external environment has on Financial Services.

The CFA charter demonstrates to employers that you have the knowledge and commitment to thrive in today's complex and evolving investment industry. The CFA level 1 qualification provides a strong foundation in real-world investment analysis and portfolio management skills, as well as emphasizing the highest ethical and professional standards. The subject areas covered by this module include: Ethics and Professional Standards; Quantitative Methods; Economics; Financial Statement Analysis; Corporate Issuers; Equities; Fixed Income; Derivatives; Alternative Investments; Portfolio Management and Wealth Planning.

This module is the first in a sequence of two Level 6 work based modules, which are designed to provide opportunities to engage in structured learning activities in the workplace. The focus of this module is on preparing apprentices to become successful finance professionals. Apprentices will develop their knowledge and skills of the systems and processes required in financial services, including learning how to analyse market data and how to communicate with internal and external clients.

This module allows students to systematically recognize reporting and accounting principles and the ability to apply them for valuation purposes. At the end of the module, students are expected to be able to create, using the appropriate software, a valuation model of a firm and critically understand the challenges in the valuation process.

This module introduces students to the fundamentals of financial technology and Python-based data analytics. Students explore key fintech sectors including payment systems, insurtech, and regulatory technology, while developing practical Python skills for financial data analysis. The course covers machine learning applications in credit scoring, fraud detection, and risk assessment. Through hands-on projects, students build real-world fintech solutions, preparing them for data-driven roles in the financial services industry.

This module combines theoretical knowledge of finance with the practical realities of modern financial markets. Students develop applied understanding of major asset classes, trading strategies, market dynamics, technical analysis, risk management, and trader decision-making in real-world contexts.

The module integrates lectures, Trading Floor Briefings, case-study discussions, and practical market exercises using real-time simulated global financial markets and industry-standard trading platforms available in the School’s trading laboratory. Students are encouraged to analyse market developments critically using a range of professional financial data sources and digital tools, including Bloomberg and alternative market platforms.

A key feature of the module is the development of evidence-based trading judgement. Students learn to formulate, defend, and evaluate trading decisions under uncertainty, integrating macroeconomic developments, market expectations, technical indicators, and risk-management principles. The module also develops students’ ability to engage critically with AI-generated financial analysis and digital market information.

The module places strong emphasis on authentic financial-market practice, communication, analytical reasoning, and reflective evaluation of trading strategies and performance.

This module will study the principles of sustainable finance, exploring the role played by financial markets and institutions in the transition to a sustainable economy. In the first part of the module, we will discuss the environment as a global public good, the prospects for using financial instruments and institutions to mitigate global externalities, and various perspectives on corporate social responsibility. In the second part, we will study the benefits and risks of ESG (environmental, social, and governance) investment, sustainable financial products, and recent developments in environmental regulation. Other topics may include the measurement of climate risk, investor preferences for sustainability, and greenwashing.

This module introduces students to the theory and practice of market design, which uses microeconomic and game-theoretic tools to construct and improve institutions for exchange and collaboration. Applications to be discussed include auction design (e.g., bidding for keywords, electromagnetic spectrum, and financial securities) and two-sided matching (e.g., school choice, the medical residency match, and organ donation). Market-design principles are now used widely to address problems faced by government and private-sector organisations, especially in the technology industry, and the module will emphasise this practical impact of the methodology.

This module introduces a selection of advanced topics in econometrics and is particularly suitable for students with an interest in pursuing empirical work at the postgraduate level. Models and techniques to be studied may include: simulation methods, quantile regression, nonparametric regression, the use of matrix algebra in regression analysis, maximum likelihood estimation, GMM estimators, panel data methods, structural change, and time series analysis, among others. The specific topics chosen in any particular year are at the discretion of the instructor.
Independent work on a topic in economics, which can be of a theoretical or applied nature, and can involve the use of any appropriate techniques

Independent work on a topic in economics, which can be of a theoretical or applied nature, and can involve the use of any appropriate techniques. Prerequisite: ECN206 or ECN211. Not open to Associate Students.

This module enhances students' empirical skills by demonstrating how to use econometric methods to analyse data in a hands-on environment. Models and techniques to be applied may include panel data, instrumental variables, and binary dependent variables, among others. The empirical questions to be addressed may be drawn from a variety of applied contexts, such as the economics of education, labour economics, political economy, macroeconomics, and the economics of crime.

This course provides an introduction to modern dynamic general equilibrium models, bridging the gap between undergraduate and postgraduate approaches to macroeconomic analysis and equipping students with essential quantitative skills. Employing a common theoretical framework to unify the treatment of different aspects of the economy, the module addresses a number of important real-world issues that are of interest to macroeconomic policy makers, central banks, traders in financial markets, and economic consultancies. Topics to be covered may include: the overlapping generations model, real business cycles, empirical analysis of macroeconomic data, real estate and mortgage markets, and the macroeconomic consequences of ageing populations.

Sustainable and unsustainable development; the economic determinants of population growth; strategies of population control; intertemporal resource management; renewable and exhaustible resources; global warming, ozone depletion and acid rain externalities and the control of pollution; economic management of forest resources; the exploitation of the sea.

Public economics explores the role of government in the economy and the design of economic policy. This module aims to develop a deep understanding of why governments intervene in markets (through taxation, regulation, and public spending) and how such interventions can be appraised and evaluated. Students will gain practical skills in economic appraisal and policy evaluation techniques, enabling them to analyse the effectiveness, efficiency, and equity of public policies in real-world contexts.

This module presents concepts, models, and data that are useful for understanding the impact of macroeconomic policies. Building on recent research into how shocks drive economic fluctuations, the module will develop analyses of conventional fiscal and monetary policy in normal times, as well as unconventional fiscal and monetary policy in the context of a liquidity trap. Topics to be covered may include: quantitative easing, forward guidance, negative interest rates, fiscal multipliers, the zero lower bound, structural reforms, and the fiscal theory of the price level. Applications may include: the response to COVID, energy price shocks, and the international transmission of financial crises. Upon completing the module, students will be able to appreciate both the theoretical and practical considerations that inform macroeconomic policy decisions and determine their impact.

This module covers the economic analysis of the labour market, including both foundational topics — labour supply and demand, human capital, discrimination — and recent developments such as early childhood education, migration, monopsony, and the origins and drivers of gender inequality. A substantial part of the course is devoted to empirical methods and their application to contemporary labour economics research, with a focus on how state-of-the-art papers test economic theory and inform policy. Students also engage critically with policy-relevant outputs, including research summaries, policy briefs, and opinion pieces.

Topics include operation of forward and futures markets; arbitrage and its application to forward and futures prices; hedging. Construction and valuation of swaps contracts. Use of options in hedging and speculation; price bounds and put-call parity; delta hedging; binomial pricing models.

This module aims to bridge the gap between undergraduate and postgraduate study of economic theory. It is therefore recommended for students who are interested in pursuing a masters degree in economics or finance, and who have achieved consistently high marks in the microeconomics core curriculum. The module will cover a number of advanced topics in microeconomics, such as: general equilibrium analysis, social choice, contract theory, games with incomplete information, auctions, networks, and matching models. The specific topics chosen in any particular year are at the discretion of the instructor.

This module covers the application of economic principles to the study of health. Topics will include the demand for health care and its supply; issues in health care finance, including uncertainty, insurance, and the rationale for public and private provision; the extent to which welfare economics can be applied to health, including definitions of inequality and the links between inequalities in income and health; overview of reforms of the health care sector; and evaluation of health care treatments (cost effectiveness and cost utility analysis).

This module explores key challenges facing developing countries. It introduces students to major topics in modern development economics, including poverty, health, education, agriculture, credit markets, and political economy.

Behavioural economics seeks to improve our understanding of economics by providing empirical evidence on how human behaviour differs from the predictions of standard models of `perfect rationality'. The module will provide an understanding of how controlled experiments can be used to study how humans make economic decisions. Students should be able to interpret and design both lab and field experiments to test economic ideas. The module will be applied and `hands-on'; we will examine real-world examples and studies from business, policy-making, personal-wellbeing, and economic development. In doing so, the module aims to enrich students' understanding of core economic concepts, and the relationship between economic theory, empirical evidence and prediction.

This module introduces students to the study of political institutions through formal models. It covers some of the major topics studied in Political Economy and Formal Political Theory: The aggregation of preferences from individual preferences to social preferences, voting, electoral competition and electoral systems, collective action, public goods, legislature voting and separation of powers.

This module examines how globalisation has transformed the scope, operations, and financial decision-making of multinational corporations. As firms increasingly operate across integrated international markets, financial management has evolved into a complex global function requiring strategic analysis and decision-making. The module focuses on three main areas: the management of foreign exchange exposure, financing multinational firms in global capital markets, and the evaluation of foreign investment decisions. The module combines theoretical foundations and academic literature with real-world case studies of multinational corporations to demonstrate how firms respond to global financial challenges in practice. Through the use of case studies, students will develop their analytical and problem-solving skills by applying financial concepts to practical business situations. By the end of the module, students will be able to evaluate the financial implications of globalisation for firms, apply analytical tools to international financial decisions, and work collaboratively to produce professional analytical reports.

This module aims to provide a critical overview of the evolution of economic theory since Adam Smith. The module focuses on how different schools of thought/economists have addressed a number of themes including where value comes from, pricing and distribution theories, the relation between finance and the real economy, the role of the government. Each school of thought/economist is critically analysed by focusing on assumptions, methods and techniques, economic problems and policy prescriptions.

The main aim of the module is to provide students with the necessary skills to perform valuation of the firms, securities and other assets. Every week during the classes, students will enhance those skills by applying appropriate valuation techniques to specific firms in real business finance case studies. The lectures and classes will make extensive use of case studies. This will allow students to come as close as possible, within a context of a classroom, to the experience of real world decision makers in corporations and investment banks, to recognise the uncertainty and the ambiguity that is present in every such decision.

This module provides a rigorous survey of key topics in portfolio management, with a focus on the practical and empirical applications of modern portfolio theory and asset pricing. We begin with a review of portfolio theory and discuss the implementation of portfolio optimisation techniques in practice. We then examine the pricing of assets in equilibrium in both single and multi-factor settings. A discussion of the consequent empirical implications will lead us into topics on active portfolio management, investment strategies, portfolio performance evaluation, and bond portfolio management. You may also have an opportunity to engage with issues in international portfolio management while working on the group project. Throughout the course, we will look at a number of case studies and work with data to get a better understanding of the practical implementation challenges associated with creating and managing large portfolios.

In this module we will learn about the sources and determinants of economic inequality. We will begin by thinking about how we should understand top income and wealth concentration: The fact that rich people are so much higher than the rest (the so-called "1%." New and old theories of income and wealth concentration will be studied. We will then switch gears and think about what generations overall inequality. Is it luck? Higher education? Having rich or better educated parents? Finally, we will take a slightly perspective and discuss how income inequality manifests itself, specifically whether income differences are mostly driven by education level, industries, or occupations.

The past few years have witnessed enormous interest in the use of large datasets and new empirical techniques to uncover patterns in financial markets. In this course, we will examine how large datasets, empirical techniques for using large datasets such as (but not limited to) machine learning, and insights from decades of finance research come together in helping market participants take decisions, and affect financial markets. The use of such techniques forms the core of modern financial institutions, especially in retail markets that interact with financial consumers such as credit markets, and quantitative asset management strategies. The primary purpose of this course is not to teach statistical methods, but to facilitate their use and the financial and economic interpretation of empirical estimates. We, therefore, will study tools and applications at the same time. At the end of the course, students will be able to use modern empirical techniques such as machine learning on large financial datasets, assess the informativeness of empirical estimates and their use in financial markets and visualize complex information sets. Students will be able to apply these tools to specific financial markets (for e.g. credit markets) and in asset management.

This module studies firm behaviour in markets and its relationship to market structure. Topics covered may include: market power, monopoly pricing, price discrimination, product selection and differentiation, advertising, market entry and exit, predation and entry deterrence, cartel formation, implicit collusion, antitrust enforcement, mergers, regulation, network effects, technological standards, research and development, and intellectual property.

This module explores the economic causes and consequences of rapid technological change, with a particular focus on 21st-century developments in machine learning and "artificial intelligence" (AI). Material to be covered may include: the economic history of major periods of innovation; the intellectual history of AI research; economic theories of the interaction between humans and technology; the macroeconomic impact of AI on growth and the distribution of income; its effects on the markets for labour, education, and health care; its broader socio-political and cultural consequences; and the use of AI tools in economics and finance research. The specific topics chosen are at the discretion of the instructor.

This module is designed to provide opportunities to engage in structured learning activities in the workplace. The focus of this module is on preparing apprentices to become successful finance professionals. Apprentices will develop the ability of strategy and planning, of autonomy in problem solving, as well as the ability to lead on the development of changes.

The aim of this module is to provide a rigorous training in the theory of investment and capital markets and a systematic understanding of its central concepts. More specifically, its purpose is to show how individuals and institutions take decisions about optimal investment and to examine the behaviour of the capital markets in which these decisions are taken. The module will also provide students with an understanding of the theory and practice of pricing and hedging derivative securities. The emphasis of the module is on studying derivatives from the point of view of industry practitioners, how derivatives are used in portfolio management, and in hedge fund strategies.

This module is specifically for students undertaking the four year Economics and Finance programmes with a year abroad. These students are the only students eligible for this module. Students must pass this module in order to progress to year 4 of the programme. The requirement to pass a year abroad module of this type shall be to take 120 and pass minimum of 105 QMUL academic credits in the assessments set by the partner institution, and to achieve a minimum year average mark of 40.0. If a student fails the module they will be transferred to the equivalent three year programme. This module wii be zero-weighted. Students can take modules both in and outside their subject-area, expanding their horizons and providing for future development.

This module will study the causes and consequences of international trade flows. To this end, we will introduce the theoretical tools needed to understand why countries trade, which goods and services are traded, what are the gains from trade and how are they distributed, and why multinational corporations exist. We will also investigate the motivation for restricting or regulating international trade, as well as the substance of trade policy. The module will combine theoretical and empirical analysis, providing students with a strong grasp of the relevant data sets and how they can be used to understand the international trading system.
A design, development or research project in the field of electronic engineering or computer science, to be taken by all final year JP/JEI students.

CBU5201 Machine Learning covers the fundamental concepts, methodology and practical tools necessary to understand, build and assess data-driven models to describe real-world systems and predict their behaviour. We will follow the standard machine learning taxonomy to organise problems and techniques into well-defined families (supervised and supervised learning) and subfamilies. We will pay particular attention to the methodology that we need to use to avoid and identify common pitfalls as well as ethics in machine learning. State-of-the-art models and the latest developments including Large Language Model (LLM) on model deployment will be discussed.

This module covers the following key concepts and themes:

Machine learning fundamentals:

Introduction to machine learning and ethics (week 1)

Methodology I and II (weeks 1 and 3)

Supervised problems and techniques:

Regression (week 1)

Classification (weeks 2 and 3)

Unsupervised problems and techniques:

Structure analysis (week 3)

Density Estimation (week 4)

Recent Topics:

Modern neural networks and deep learning (week 3)

LLM and Deployment (week 4)

This module provides an introduction to OO programming and the Java language, both of which are new to the students. It covers a range of key concepts necessary to program in Java including loops, conditional statements and data structures; also more advanced concepts such as the manipulation of files and building Graphical User Interfaces (GUI).

Syllabus

Teaching Block 1 – Java

Introduction to OO in Java

Classes and objects, access modifiers, variable scope and methods, constructors

Arrays and ArrayLists

Java API brief intro

Teaching Block 2 – Java

Inheritance

Interfaces & Abstract classes

Object class

Teaching Block 3 – Java

Garbage Collection (GC)

Strings & Numbers

Exceptions & Assertions

File I/O

Collections & Sorting

Basic GUI

Teaching Block 4 – Python

OO concepts for Python

Inheritance, Polymorphism & Abstract classes in Python

OO tools & Data Handling

The course provides a comprehensive understanding of the fundamental concepts and methods behind artificial intelligence (AI) and the key AI applications. The course covers the fundamental, but most important developments of AI supporting decision making while touching upon the ethics and safety of AI.

The key focus is placed on a range of topics, including acquiring and representing human knowledge, development and functioning of AI systems, implementation of fundamental AI techniques, AI Applications, Ethics and Safety of AI, and exploration of key philosophical issues underlying AI.

This module is designed to equip students with practical skills and an understanding of the underlying principles of programming the World Wide Web. There will be two hours of lectures per week, and weekly timetabled lab sessions for each student. Major topics include:
1. Internet and Web server basics
2. Client-side programming using HTML5, Cascading Style Sheets, and JavaScript
3. Server-side programming using PHP
4. Practical issues on setting up a website

Interactive objects are increasingly appearing in computing and interactive art domains including tangible computing and embedded objects. The module provides students with skills, knowledge, and experience of designing and prototyping interactive physical objects using contemporary microcontrollers. The module covers basic electronics, control circuits, sensors (analogue and digital), output (analogue and digital),microcontrollers, simple networking, and microcontroller programming using the popular Arduino open-source platform. It additionally touches on topics of interaction design and evaluation to provide a framework in which students can prototype and understand interactive objects.

This module introduces modern software development techniques essential for building high-quality software and managing its development effectively. Students will gain hands-on experience in advanced programming and team-based development, with a strong emphasis on communication and collaboration throughout the software lifecycle. Key topics include understanding customer requirements, analysis and design, collaborative development practices, the use of modern tools, writing clean and maintainable code, software testing, and addressing key challenges in project management and professional ethics.

The module provides principles and techniques of interactive media design and production using conventional media processing tools. It covers the following topics: elements of cognitive psychology, visual perception, human factors in multimedia design, design principles and design process, animation and interactivity, colour perception, use of the media, usability and heuristic evaluation, image formats, digital and web video, principles of video interaction. JavaScript and HTML/CSS are also used to produce interactive multimedia content in the labs via mini-projects.

This course introduces students to core principles and practices of enterprise management. It covers fundamental concepts, strategies, and tools used in managing complex organizations. The course emphasizes practical application of theories to real-world business scenarios, with a focus on technology-driven industries. Through case studies and examples from the global business landscape, students will develop a comprehensive understanding of modern enterprise management challenges and solutions.

Course Outline (12 weeks - taught in 5 day blocks x 4 weeks). The module webpages indicate specific topics taught per block

Introduction to Enterprise Management

Business Environment Analysis

Organizational Structure

Business Strategies: Strategic Analysis and Strategic Planning

Financial Management and Accounting Basics

Marketing in the Digital Age

Operations and Supply Chain Management

Human Resource Management

Risk Management

Globalization and International Business

Ethics, Corporate Social Responsibility, and Sustainability

Future Trends in Enterprise Management

This module provides an introduction to generative systems through creative coding. Students will locate this creativity in the history of computer-generated art/design and understand the role of algorithms to generate complex systems. Students will learn how code can be used to create their visual outputs, initially through exploring features in programming languages or libraries designed to support creativity. By then incorporating physics principles, students will add complexity to their systems, through e.g. emergence, autonomy and fractals.

This module is an introduction to the representation, analysis, and processing of digital images. It covers topics such as sampling and quantisation, human vision, colour models, image representations, encoding and compression, and image processing. The main methods of delivery are lectures, exercises, labs, and tutorials.

Innovation and technology are powerful, interconnected forces that shape the world around us. Innovation drives progress, while technology turns those ideas into practical applications that transform industries and improve everyday lives. This module explores how innovation drives technological development and how engineering harnesses both to address real-world challenges. Through a hands-on approach, students will explore how innovation and technology drive progress, foster sustainable development, and shape the future of engineering.

This module introduces students to the principles of network security and how they are applied in real-world communication systems. You will learn about encryption, authentication, and protocols that protect the confidentiality and integrity of data across the Internet and modern networks. The course also provides a foundation in cryptography and highlights current technologies and threats.

Indicative topics include:

Introduction to Network Security – key concepts, threats, classical ciphers, and cryptanalysis.

Symmetric Encryption – DES, AES, block cipher modes, and key management.

Public-Key Cryptography – RSA, Diffie-Hellman, hash functions, digital signatures.

Authentication Protocols – Kerberos, X.509, and user authentication techniques.

Secure Architectures – IPSec, firewalls, VPNs, trusted systems.

Web and Application Security – TLS 1.3, HTTPS, OAuth2, secure sessions.

Email and Messaging Security – PGP, S/MIME, and modern secure messaging.

Emerging Topics – optional content may include post-quantum cryptography, IoT and cloud security, or case studies on current threats.

The Fourier Transform (FT), is discussed in detail in the module Digital Signal Processing. It is applied in several time/frequency analysis applications. However, the application of the FT is limited to stationary signals, since time information in the time domain is lost in the frequency domain. This module briefly revises the FT, linear algebra and the multi-variable statistical technique Principal Component Analysis (PCA). The module then introduces non-stationary signals and investigates methods of retaining the time information in the transform. Time-frequency analysis techniques are discussed in some detail, and explores how they are suitable for different signal and image processing applications such as filtering and compression. These techniques include the Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT), Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT), Wavelet Transform (WT), Wigner-Ville Distribution (WVD) and Karhunen-Loeve Transform (KLT).

Linear Algebra

Fourier Transform

Discrete Cosine Transform

Uncertainty Principle

Short-Time Fourier Transform

Karhunen-Loeve Transform

Haar Functions

Multiresolution Analysis

Wavelet Transform

Wigner-Ville Distribution

Perfect Reconstruction

Practical Applications

This course offers a comprehensive introduction to 3D graphics, focusing on the software tools integral to the design of virtual environments and games. Covering an array of key topics, from 3D object modelling and camera models to transformations and lighting, the course provides a detailed look at the intricacies of clipping and rasterization. Students will gain a solid understanding of the programming tools that are most relevant to 3D graphics, particularly through the practical application of OpenGL. The curriculum is designed not only to impart knowledge of basic transformations and rendering techniques but also to enable students to create their own computer-generated animations. This blend of theory and hands-on practice prepares students to confidently navigate and create within the dynamic realm of 3D graphics.

1: geometric primitives, modelling, modelling transformations, camera models
Learn the basic elements in OpenGL practice including basic commands, shapes, as well introductory case studies. Understand different types of viewing angles, events, and animation. Basic 3D drawing will also be introduced.

2: Viewing and projection transformations, lighting calculations, textures
Gain understanding of the advanced programming techniques for OpenGL. Practise interactive events. Get familiar with how light and colours can be applied in the modelling process. Understand how cameras and transformations can be implemented and adjusted programmatically.

3: programming tools for virtual reality
Understand the theories that go behind the modelling process with OpenGL for virtual reality

4: programming tools for augmented reality
Gain in-depth understanding of different types of programming tools and usage for augmented reality

During this module, you will learn a range of Artificial Intelligence techniques employed in games, as well as how games can be used for research in Artificial Intelligence. During this module, you will learn how to program agents to play different types of games in both single- and multi-player settings. The module gives an overview of multiple techniques, and it is organised in two blocks: Search and Decision Making, and Reinforcement Learning. In the first part, you will learn the basics of Search, reasoning, and adversarial games and how they are applied to games in different algorithms. In the second part, you will learn the principles of Reinforcement Learning and Deep Learning applied to games. The entire module is very practical and includes a number of programming assignments, guided exercises, and tutorials.

This module is largely driven by the recognition that effective visual perception is crucial in understanding intelligent behavior. This module covers theoretical knowledge and applications of computer vision that is based on machine learning techniques. Computer vision techniques , such as features, correspondence, filtering, segmentation, classification, tracking, and recognition will be introduced to students together with the usage of machine learning.

The course provides a comprehensive understanding of the representation, analysis, and processing of digital multimedia. Topics include sampling, quantisation, colour/sound/image/video representation and compression (JPEG, MPEG, MP3), and elements of psychoacoustics, vision, and multimedia networking.

Students will gain practical skills in multimedia encoding and editing, and critical evaluation, alongside theoretical foundations in digital signal processing. Delivered through asynchronous activities (lecture notes, exercises, quizzes), synchronous lectures/tutorials, the course is an essential building block for students aiming to excel in the field of multimedia technology, providing the theoretical knowledge and practical expertise needed to succeed in the industry.

Today, many technologies are designed to be used in a dynamic, changing context; and their primary use is often social interaction and fun i.e. there is no quantifiable output and no clear goal other than enjoyment. Computer games, mobile music players and online communities are all examples where the quality of the experience is the primary aim of the interaction, and usage is highly dependent on social context. Computer usage is also shifting away from the traditional keyboard/screen paradigm towards mobile, multimodal, wearable and ubiquitous systems.

This course explores the challenges these new technologies, and the industries they have created, present for the design and evaluation of interactive systems. It moves away from the traditional human-computer interaction model with its focus on increasing efficiency or minimizing errors for single users, and explores theories relating to usability and experience, social context, creativity and live performance. It explores the nature of engagement with interactive systems and between people when mediated by interactive systems.

Generative artificial intelligence (or generative AI) is a subset of artificial intelligence that uses generative models to produce artefacts and creative content such as text, audio, images, videos, or other forms of data. Its practitioners work at the cutting edge of artificial intelligence, building assistive tools and autonomous systems, inspired by work both in computer science and in allied fields like psychology, sociology, and many creative practices. Through a mix of lectures, practical tutorials, and discussion groups, we will explore the theory, applications, and philosophy underpinning Generative AI. We will learn how to use a range of artificial intelligence techniques, from VAEs and GANs to Diffusion Models and transformer-based LLMs, to build computationally creative software and explore some exciting applications in software development, science, finance, entertainment, marketing and advertising, art, writing, fashion, and product design (among others). Over the course of the module, you will also undertake a personal project to implement or develop a Generative AI system. This project will allow you to put your theoretical and practical lessons into action and to explore your own ideas and views about the field.

This module addresses autonomous systems that reason about their own actions and about the environment and context they operate in, treating robotics as an embodied perception, decision and action discipline rather than fixed automation. Building on the machine learning, computer vision and agent reasoning students have already met, it develops the numerical and computational methods needed to embed those techniques in a physical robot: kinematics, probabilistic state estimation, planning, and learned control. Established algorithms and autonomy models form the basis for study, and students design and evaluate such a system in simulation as part of their coursework project. Theory and practice are linked through simulation exercises and through discussion of real systems, from warehouse mobile robots to surgical robots and recent vision-language-action models. Safety, ethics and inclusive design for users of differing physical and cognitive abilities are treated as engineering requirements throughout.

Cognitive robots and how to program them: cognition and cognitive mechanisms, cognitive modelling, embodiment, and simulation-based robot programming in simulated and real environemnts.

Robot modelling and mechanics: rigid-body transformations, forward and inverse kinematics of serial manipulators, parallel manipulators and legged robots, mobile robot models.

Perception, state estimation and navigation: sensors, actuators and data fusion; recursive Bayesian estimation (Kalman, extended Kalman and particle filters); localisation, path planning and SLAM.

Learning for robots: sensorimotor mappings and coordination, learning eye-hand coordination, deep-learning visual perception, imitation learning and reinforcement learning, with attention to data, evaluation, sim-to-real transfer and safe deployment.

Cognitive architectures and embodied AI: robot cognitive architectures for problem solving, human-centred and inclusive system design, and recent vision-language and vision-language-action approaches.

This module will provide an in-depth exploration of optical-based transmission systems and networks. In Week 1, we’ll cover the fundamentals of optical fibers, including their structures and key transmission characteristics. Week 2 will focus on optical communication systems, including sources, receivers, amplifiers, and modulators, with hands-on simulations. In Weeks 3 and 4, we’ll delve into optical network architectures, standards, and technologies, including Passive Optical Networks (PONs) and essential networking components.

This module provides students with a comprehensive understanding of modern wireless technologies, encompassing advanced antenna design, MIMO systems, and beamforming, as well as the evolution and architecture of 4G LTE/LTE-A and 5G New Radio (NR). Students will study 5G requirements, spectrum, and enabling technologies such as massive MIMO, mmWave, network densification, beam sweeping, heterogeneous small cells, and massive IoT. Students also investigate advanced emerging technologies, including cooperative communications, energy harvesting, and non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA), with an emphasis on modelling, performance analysis, and applications. Through a blend of theory, practical insights, and case studies, this module equips students with the expertise required for careers in the rapidly evolving field of wireless engineering.

1. Antennas and Propagation:
Key Antenna Parameters; Friis Transmission Eqn; Antenna Design Techniques; Antennas for Satellite Communications; MIMO Antenna for 5G Communications.

2. Massive MIMO, Phased Array and Beamforming:
MIMO Channel; Channel Mathematical Model; MIMO Spatial Diversity Techniques; Massive MIMO; Beamforming Techniques; Beam Division Multiple Access Techniques used in 5G; Beam Steering; and Smart/Phased Array Antennas.

3. Preliminaries and Standards of Emerging Technologies:
5G Service and Network Evolution; Network Densification and Heterogeneous Small Cells, MmWave, Massive IoT, Error Rate Analysis of modulation techniques; Physical Channel Processing, OFDM and SC-FDMA; 5G New Radio (NR): Numerology and Frame Structure, Initial Access and Beam Sweeping, Physical Channels and Signals.

4. Emerging Wireless Technologies:
Cooperative Communications, Energy Harvesting, NOMA, mmWave, and Case Studies.

This module immerses students in the foundations of embedded systems design, with a primary focus on the ARM Cortex-M4 architecture and STM32 microcontrollers. Students will develop essential competencies in low-level programming using assembly language and C, mastering key concepts such as memory organisation, comprehensive peripheral interfacing—including GPIO, ADC, timers, interrupts, DMA, UART, I2C, and SPI—and real-time operating systems using FreeRTOS. The learning experience is structured around a GenAI-empowered Conceive–Design–Implement–Operate (CDIO) framework, supported by authentic, challenge-based assessments. Through intensive, hands-on project work, students will cultivate critical engineering skills, including debugging, system integration, and collaborative development, by applying their knowledge to build complex embedded applications. Students will develop their professional engineering identity by working as individual engineers within a team-based embedded-systems development context. They will take responsibility for technical decisions, contribute accountably to shared system integration, communicate and justify design choices, validate system behaviour, and reflect on how their individual work affects the overall engineering outcome. This approach fosters critical thinking and reflective learning, responsible human–AI collaboration, professional responsibility, and evidence-based engineering judgement, preparing students for industry-relevant design workflows and equipping them with the higher-order skills essential for real-world engineering practice.

EBU6502 Cloud Computing module introduces students to "Hardware-as-a-Software" concept based on virtualisation technologies to deploy large-scale distributed systems remotely within a very short time, saving you time and money, compared to deploying conventional IT infrastructures using physical hardware in data centres. Cloud Computing is the on-demand "pay-as-you-go" model of providing IT resources (compute, storage, databases, software, networking, etc) as a service and be charged only for the amount of resources you have used. The module will consist of class lectures and hands-on labs.

Cloud computing is to represent the future of modern computing. This module provides students adequate information on the basic topics of cloud computing, such as cloud infrastructure, service oriented architectures, data storage and protocols. This module also introduces current platforms, social networking and explores the managing and security issues. This module contains practical topics requiring students to understand how to develop applications on the cloud using the application programming interfaces(APIs) and Amazon Web Services (AWS) virtual resources and services such as the Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2), Elastic Load Balancer (ELB) and CloudWatch.

The main contents of this modules are:

Cloud Computing Fundamentals
Service Level Agreements (SLAs) and Virtualization
The Economics of Cloud Computing
Cloud Scalability
Cloud Security and Trust
Creating and Managing AWS EC2 Instances
GPU Programming and CUDA Model
Enterprise Design Paterns and Monitoring Systems
Big Data and Map Reduce (Hadoop) Processing Techniques
Data Centre Design and Implementation
Ethics in Cloud Computing

This course core challenges facing the increasingly smart infrastructures that significantly improve their operational functions and through data analytics, statistical methods and machine learning algorithms. The key focus is placed on five different area of smart applications: 1) mobility and transportation; 2) building energy and power grid systems; 3) extreme events and urban resilience;4) climate change and environmental variability; and 5) Digital Twins as a virtual model.

1: Introduction and motivation
2: Data analytics for smart infrastructures
3: Urban smart infrastructure (system) theory
4: Application 1: Mobility and transportation
5: Application 2: Building energy and power grid systems
6: Application 3: Smart systems for healthcare
7: Application 4: Climate change and smart agriculture
8: Application 5: Digital twin – a virtual model

This module introduces both the classical/symoblic intelligent systems for reaasoning and modern LLM-based reasoning and agentic systems.

Reinforcement Learning: Covers MDPs, value functions, Bellman backups, Q-learning, SARSA, exploration strategies and deep reinforcement learning.

Knowledge Representation: Covers entities, relations, attributes, triples, identifiers, schema graphs and structured agent memory.

Knowledge Graph Foundations: Covers graph construction, multi-hop reasoning, entity resolution, provenance, freshness and context retrieval.

Knowledge Graphs in Modern AI: Covers RAG, neuro-symbolic AI, multimodal reasoning, MCP, tool use and multi-agent coordination.

Coding Agents: Covers planner-coder-tester-reviewer workflows, repository graphs, impact analysis, agent memory and safety controls.

Bayesian Networks: Covers directed acyclic graphs, conditional probability tables, conditional independence and d-separation.

Exact Inference: Covers enumeration, factor operations, variable elimination, normalisation, elimination order and treewidth.

Probabilistic Reasoning over Time: Covers filtering, prediction, smoothing, Viterbi reasoning, HMMs, Kalman filters and DBNs.

Planning with Uncertainty: Covers utility, expected utility, value of information, decision networks, MDPs, value iteration and policy iteration.

DDNs and POMDPs: Covers dynamic decision networks, belief updates, action-observation loops, POMDPs and belief-state planning.

Inference-Time Decoding Controls: Explores temperature, top-p, maximum tokens, and stop sequences for controlling LLM outputs.

Reasoning Techniques for LLMs: Introduces prompting engineering for LLM reasoning, such as Chain-of-Thought, self-consistency, and reasoning evaluation.

Classical Search for Problem Solving: Covers BFS, DFS, UCS, A*, and beam search for systematic problem solving.

Test-Time Compute for LLM Reasoning: Examines Tree of Thoughts, Best-of-N sampling, and reward-guided beam search.

Post-Training for LLM Reasoning: Explains reinforcement learning fine-tuning, especially GRPO, for improving reasoning capabilities of LLMs.

LLM-Based Agents: Introduces ReAct, tool use, feedback loops, coding agents, and iterative agentic workflows.

This module provides theoretical and empirical knowledge of the well-established techniques in computer vision principles, as well as recent techniques such as deep learning-based computer vision. The module aims to cover core concepts, including classical computer vision techniques, deep learning fundamentals and deep learning-based techniques for computer vision tasks.

[Unit 1] Classical computer vision and machine learning - 1
- Restoration / Feature detection / Fitting / Grouping / Calibration / Epipolar /Stereo matching
[Unit 2] Classical computer vision and machine learning - 2
- Tracking / ML Basics / Classification / Detection
[Unit 3] Deep learning fundamentals
- Loss, Backpropagation, CNN, Attention, Transformers, VLM (CLIP), etc
[Unit 4] Deep learning for computer vision
- Deep learning for classification/detection/tracking/segmentation/generation, safe AI

EBU6502 Cloud Computing module introduces students to "Hardware-as-a-Software" concept based on virtualisation technologies to deploy large-scale distributed systems remotely within a very short time, saving you time and money, compared to deploying conventional IT infrastructures using physical hardware in data centres. Cloud Computing is the on-demand "pay-as-you-go" model of providing IT resources (compute, storage, databases, software, networking, etc) as a service and be charged only for the amount of resources you have used. The module will consist of class lectures and hands-on labs.

Cloud computing is to represent the future of modern computing. This module provides students adequate information on the basic topics of cloud computing, such as cloud infrastructure, service oriented architectures, data storage and protocols. This module also introduces current platforms, social networking and explores the managing and security issues. This module contains practical topics requiring students to understand how to develop applications on the cloud using the application programming interfaces(APIs) and Amazon Web Services (AWS) virtual resources and services such as the Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2), Elastic Load Balancer (ELB) and CloudWatch.

The main contents of this modules are:

Cloud Computing Fundamentals
Service Level Agreements (SLAs) and Virtualization
The Economics of Cloud Computing
Cloud Scalability
Cloud Security and Trust
Creating and Managing AWS EC2 Instances
GPU Programming and CUDA Model
Enterprise Design Paterns and Monitoring Systems
Big Data and Map Reduce (Hadoop) Processing Techniques
Data Centre Design and Implementation
Ethics in Cloud Computing

This module introduces the fundamental principles of cybersecurity and artificial intelligence. It explores key concepts in security, encryption, authentication, and secure coding before examining the main approaches in AI, including modern data-driven machine learning. In its final part, the module considers the dual relationship between AI and security —how AI can enhance protection yet introduce new risks— and reflects on the ethical, legal, and societal implications of developing secure and trustworthy intelligent systems.

This is an introductory module in computer programming using Java. You will learn the basic concepts of programming and learn to write and reason about simple programs. The main topics covered are: storing and manipulating data, control structures, methods and recursion, and algorithms for searching and sorting data. Classes include weekly lectures and lab sessions. You will be assessed by coursework throughout the term and by an end-of-term exam. Both will require you to demonstrate that you can write programs and understand theory.

This compulsory module covers the basic concepts in communications and networks. It introduces the concept of a communications system and then focusses on specific elements. It covers circuit and switched versus packet switched networks, and the ISO/OSI 7 layer model. Also covered are certain critical network protocols, e.g. TCP/IP and CSMA/CD, key Internet concepts, converged networks, and mobile networks.

This module provides you with a basic understanding of how a computer works and how programs are executed by the CPU at the machine level. As an introduction to computer architecture and systems software, this module presents the concepts needed to understand typical computers at the level of their ';machine-code'; instruction set. It covers Boolean algebra rules and terminology as well as logic gates. The module also examines the use of bits, bytes and data formats to represent integers, text and programs as well as looking at the conventional von Neumann computer architecture (CPU, registers, memory). Assembly language programming and system software are introduced.

This module will introduce programming to students through designing and building arts applications. Students will learn to build graphics-based applications using Processing and audio applications using Java. By focussing on the range of applications that can be built, students will learn programming skills. The focus on this module is as much on the creativity of ideas as on how to write code to realise these ideas.

The module consists of two parts, each of fundamental importance for any serious approach to Computer Science: Logic and Discrete Structures. Logic has been called the Calculus of Computer Science. It plays a very important role in computer architecture (logic gates), software engineering (specification and verification), programming languages (semantics, logic programming), databases (relational algebra and SQL the standard computer language for accessing and manipulating databases), artificial intelligence (automatic theorem proving), algorithms (complexity and expressiveness), and theory of computation (general notions of computability). Computer scientists use Discrete Mathematics to think about their subject and to communicate their ideas independently of particular computers and programs. They expect other computer scientists to be fluent in the language and methods of Discrete Mathematics. In the module we consider Propositional logic as well as Predicate Calculus. We will treat Propositional Logic and Predicate Calculus as formal systems. You will learn how to produce and annotate formal proofs. As application we will briefly consider the programming language Prolog. This module will also cover a variety of standard representations, operations, properties, constructions and applications associated with selected structures from Discrete Mathematics (sets, relations, functions, directed graphs, orders).

Mathematics primarily for electrical and electronic engineers. Purely a techniques module, involving several topics with variable amounts of overlap. Differentiation and applications, partial derivatives. Integration and applications. Vectors, complex numbers, series.

This is a Level 4 module introducing you to electronic devices, components, circuits and simple systems. There is particular emphasis on the basic theorems and techniques of electric circuit theory in relation to simple a.c. and d.c. circuits in order to provide a sound theoretical background to both analogue and digital modules in subsequent semesters.

This first year module introduces the fundamentals of signals, Fourier Series, information theory and signal statistics. Topics covered include: signal fundamentals such as discrete versus continuous time signals; signal average, energy and power; orthogonality; Fourier Series. The module also provides an introduction to information theory, including the Shannon-Hartley theorem. Basic ideas in statistics will also be introduced. It will be taught by a combination of lectures, tutorials and labs.
The module covers: Number Systems and Codes; Boolean Algebra and Basic Logic Functions; MAP minimisation; Combinational Logic; Synchronous Sequential Logic; VHDL

Major topics include the concepts of class, object, method, subclass, inheritance and their use in programming. The relevance of the object oriented style with respect to concrete software problems will be stressed both in lectures and labs. There will be two hours of lectures per week, and each student will have a weekly timetabled lab session. In addition, you will be expected to spend further time outside scheduled lab periods in the lab (or at home machines if they are available), and to read textbooks and review notes.

This is a module designed to offer you practical skills as well as understanding of underlying principles of programming the World Wide Web. There will be two hours of lectures per week, and weekly timetabled lab sessions for each student. Major topics you will study include Internet and Web server basics; client-side programming using XHTML; Cascading Style Sheets, and Javascript. You will develop practical skills in server-side programming using PHP and gain an understanding and hands on experience in the practical issues involved when setting up a website.

The course locates the design methods and the development of computer systems in the wider context of the use of information technology and its impact upon organisations. The topics covered are: What are Information Systems and requirements. Why is analysis needed. Systems theory and types of information systems; their relationship with organisational processes and structures. Stakeholders. Requirements analysis and project failures Elicitation of Requirements. Techniques for eliciting requirements; user participation. Impact on project success. Object-Oriented Analysis Techniques. UML notation, including use cases and class diagrams. Overview of the software development processes. Soft Systems Methodology. Introduction to SSM and the limitation of conventional systems analysis.

Automata and formal languages are fundamental concepts in Computer Science. Automata are abstract machines that are used for representing computational processes in a mathematically precise fashion. Moreover, any device interacting with the outside world, whether a simple program or a complex system, requires well-defined, formal input and output languages. We will study automata and their relationship with formal languages and grammars.

Module will cover topics in engineering mathematics relevant to Electronics and Electrical Engineering programs: Vector Calculus (field theory, surface and volume integration, field operators), linear algebra (matrices and matrix operations, applications to systems of equations, reduced Row Echelon Form, determinants, Cramer's rule, eigenvalues and eigenvectors), differential equations (solving first and second order DEs).

This module provides you with the opportunity to examine the role of engineering in society and the expectations of society for a professional engineer. During the module, you should develop and achieve a level of written and spoken communication expected of a professional engineer. You will also construct a personal development plan (PDP) and an on-going employability skills folder. The assessment of the module is 100 per cent coursework, broken down as follows: oral presentation: 25 per cent; in-class essay: 25 per cent; PDP folder: 25 per cent; employability folder: 25 per cent. Not open to Associate Students or students from other departments.

This module provides an introduction to concepts of algorithms, programming logic, and coding for computational problem solving using a high level programming language. The module introduces the processes associated with problem solving using a programming platform and how to think algorithmically to solve programming problems efficiently. The module presents basic data types and programming structures covering unidimensional and multi-dimension variables, statements, control flow, functions, data structures, and file processing. The module stresses the importance and principles of computer algorithm design and structured programming techniques as a discipline for developing quality software programs. The pace and syllabus of the module are designed with an emphasis on producing clear, robust, and reasonably efficient small scale code using top-down design, informal analysis, and reasonably efficient testing and debugging.

This module provides you with a basic understanding of how a computer works and how programs are executed by the CPU at the machine level. As an introduction to computer architecture and systems software, this module presents the concepts needed to understand typical computers at the level of their ';machine-code'; instruction set. It covers Boolean algebra rules and terminology as well as logic gates. The module also examines the use of bits, bytes and data formats to represent integers, text and programs as well as looking at the conventional von Neumann computer architecture (CPU, registers, memory). Assembly language programming and system software are introduced.

The module gives an introduction to basic circuit modelling techniques, simulation, prototyping and measurements using bench-top and virtual (software-based) instruments. The module will cover Ohm's Law, Kirchoff's Circuit Laws, characterisation of linear and non-linear components, analogue and digital signals, power sources, lab safety. Students will work in groups on a range of short, small-scale projects, which will be assessed through group demos and presentations.
The module will also discuss topics in professional ethics in engineering practice based on published code of practice by the Royal Academy of Engineering and the IET; sustainability challenges for electronic design and in particular-e-waste and end-of-product recycling; and topics in project management. A range of tasks will guide the students through literature research and technical writing process, thus developing the competence in technical writing - a key employability skill.

This module introduces the principles of C Programming to students who already know how to program at a basic level in Java. It provides a knowledge of the theory of C Programming and also its practical use in real engineering systems. The focus is on microprocessor based systems.

This module examines the structure, applications and programming of microcontroller and similar devices. There will be practical work on using the devices as part of the module. Aims: * To impart an understanding of the architectures of microcontrollers microprocessors, and PIC devices. * To impart an understanding of the design issues in using microcontrollers and similar devices. * To enable students to make an informed choice of microcontrollers or similar device for a particular application. * To enable students to use microcontroller devices in electronic circuits.

This module covers the basic laws of electric and magnetic fields, their application to elementary problems involving steady and time changing fields and currents, and an introduction to electromagnetic radiation. The Maxwell Equations, which explain the relationships between time varying electric and magnetic fields, will be introduced. The emphasis is on physical intuition and visualisation supported by mathematical modelling and analysis and labs.

Software Engineering is concerned with applying engineering principles to the production of software. This module provides the management principles, theoretical foundations, tools, notation and background necessary to develop and test large-scale software systems. The practical part of the module consists of lab assignments in which students use a range of relevant tools (a Java programming IDE, unit testing tool, configuration management tool, UML design tool, and project planning tool).
